lessons.title: Functions and Their Graphs
lessons.content:
Imagine a juice machine at a shop in New Market. You drop in one mango, press a button, and out comes one glass of mango juice. You drop in a guava, and out comes guava juice. The machine never gives you two different glasses for the same fruit. That machine is exactly what mathematicians call a function. Calculus is the maths of change, and before we can study how things change, we need a clean way to describe how one thing depends on another. Functions are that clean way, so this whole course is built on top of them.

What a function is: A function is a rule that takes an input and gives exactly one output. We usually write it as y = f(x). Here x is the input, f is the name of the rule, and f(x) is the output. If f(x) = 2x + 1, then f(3) = 2 times 3 plus 1 = 7. The key word is "exactly one". An input can never produce two outputs. But two different inputs are allowed to give the same output. For example, if g(x) = x², then g(2) = 4 and g(-2) = 4. That is fine, because each input still has just one answer.

The vertical line test: When you draw a function on a graph, there is a quick check. Draw any vertical line. If it ever crosses the curve more than once, the curve is not a function of x, because one x would have two y values. A circle like x² + y² = 25 fails this test. The vertical line x = 3 hits it at y = 4 and y = -4. So the full circle is not a function, but the top half, y = √(25 - x²), is.

Domain and range: The domain is the set of all inputs the function is allowed to take. The range is the set of all outputs it actually produces. Think of the juice machine again: the domain is the list of fruits it accepts, and the range is the list of juices it can make. For f(x) = √x, you cannot take the square root of a negative number using real numbers, so the domain is x ≥ 0. The outputs are also never negative, so the range is y ≥ 0. For h(x) = 1/(x - 2), the only problem is x = 2, where we would divide by zero. So the domain is all real numbers except 2.

How to find a domain quickly: Look for three danger signs. First, division: the bottom must not be zero. Second, even roots like square roots: the inside must be zero or positive. Third, logarithms: the inside must be strictly positive. For example, for f(x) = ln(x - 1) / (x - 3), we need x - 1 > 0, so x > 1, and we need x ≠ 3. The domain is x > 1 with x ≠ 3. In interval notation we write (1, 3) ∪ (3, ∞). Round brackets mean the end point is not included, square brackets mean it is.

Polynomial functions: These are built from powers of x with whole number exponents, like f(x) = 3x³ - 2x + 5. The highest power is called the degree. A degree 1 polynomial is a straight line, like y = 2x + 1, where 2 is the slope and 1 is where it cuts the y axis. A degree 2 polynomial is a parabola, the U shape you see when a ball is thrown. Polynomials are friendly: their domain is all real numbers and their graphs are smooth with no breaks or sharp corners.

Rational functions: A rational function is one polynomial divided by another, like r(x) = (x + 1)/(x - 2). Their graphs can have breaks where the bottom becomes zero. Near x = 2, the value of r(x) shoots up or down without limit, and the graph hugs an invisible vertical line called a vertical asymptote. As x becomes very large, r(x) gets close to 1, so y = 1 is a horizontal asymptote. We will learn exactly how to find these with limits in the next lessons.

Exponential functions: An exponential function has the variable in the power, like f(x) = 2^x. It doubles every time x goes up by 1: 2^0 = 1, 2^1 = 2, 2^2 = 4, 2^10 = 1024. The most important base in calculus is the number e, about 2.71828. The function e^x is special because its rate of change equals itself, which we will prove later. Exponentials describe things like bacteria growing, money growing with compound interest, and viral posts spreading on Facebook. The domain is all real numbers and the range is y > 0, because 2^x is never zero or negative.

Logarithmic functions: The logarithm is the undo button of the exponential. If 2^5 = 32, then log base 2 of 32 = 5. The natural log, written ln x, is the log with base e, so ln(e) = 1 and ln(1) = 0. Its domain is x > 0. Three rules you will use again and again: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b, ln(a/b) = ln a - ln b, and ln(a^n) = n ln a. In computer science, log base 2 tells you how many times you can halve something, which is why binary search on 1024 items needs only about 10 steps.

Trigonometric functions: Sine, cosine and tangent come from angles in a right triangle, but in calculus we treat them as functions of a real number, with angles measured in radians. A full circle is 2π radians, which is 360 degrees, so π radians equals 180 degrees. Sine and cosine repeat every 2π, so we call them periodic with period 2π. Their range is from -1 to 1. Tangent, tan x = sin x / cos x, repeats every π and is undefined where cos x = 0, such as x = π/2. Always use radians in calculus. Many formulas, like the derivative of sin x being cos x, are only true in radians.

Inverse functions: An inverse function runs the machine backwards. If f(x) = 2x + 1, then to undo it we subtract 1 and divide by 2, so f⁻¹(x) = (x - 1)/2. Check: f(3) = 7 and f⁻¹(7) = 3. A function has an inverse only if it is one-to-one, meaning different inputs always give different outputs. The horizontal line test checks this: no horizontal line may cross the graph twice. The graph of an inverse is the mirror image of the original across the line y = x. Inverse trigonometric functions like sin⁻¹ x work only after we restrict sine to a range where it is one-to-one, from -π/2 to π/2.

Composition of functions: Composition means feeding the output of one function into another. We write (f ∘ g)(x) = f(g(x)). If g(x) = x + 3 and f(x) = x², then f(g(x)) = (x + 3)², while g(f(x)) = x² + 3. These are different, so order matters. A nice picture is a factory line: first the cloth is cut, then it is stitched. Swapping the order gives a mess. Composition becomes very important when we learn the chain rule for derivatives.

Even and odd functions: A function is even if f(-x) = f(x) for every x. Its graph is symmetric about the y axis, like a butterfly. Examples are x², x⁴ and cos x. A function is odd if f(-x) = -f(x). Its graph has rotational symmetry about the origin. Examples are x, x³ and sin x. Most functions are neither. Why care? Later, when we integrate an odd function from -a to a, the answer is always zero, which saves a lot of work in exams.

Transformations of graphs: Once you know a basic graph, you can move it around. y = f(x) + 3 shifts the graph up by 3. y = f(x - 2) shifts it right by 2, which surprises many students because of the minus sign. y = -f(x) flips it upside down across the x axis. y = 2f(x) stretches it vertically by 2. With these four moves, you can sketch y = (x - 2)² + 3 instantly: it is the basic parabola moved right 2 and up 3, so its lowest point is at (2, 3).

Piecewise functions and absolute value: Sometimes a rule changes depending on the input. The absolute value |x| is defined as x when x ≥ 0 and -x when x < 0. So |5| = 5 and |-5| = 5. Its graph is a V shape with a sharp corner at zero. Another example is a mobile data package: up to 1 GB you pay one rate, after that a different rate. Piecewise functions are where many interesting calculus questions about limits and continuity come from.

Real life example 1, the rickshaw fare: Suppose a rickshaw puller in Mirpur charges 20 taka to start plus 15 taka per kilometre. The fare is a function: F(d) = 20 + 15d, where d is distance in kilometres. Step 1, the domain: distance cannot be negative, and realistically it is at most maybe 10 km, so 0 ≤ d ≤ 10. Step 2, the output: F(2) = 20 + 30 = 50 taka. Step 3, the inverse: if you have 80 taka, how far can you go? Solve 80 = 20 + 15d, so d = 4 km. That inverse is F⁻¹(y) = (y - 20)/15. You just used a linear function, its domain, and its inverse in one rickshaw ride.

Real life example 2, a phone battery: Your phone battery loses charge in a way that is roughly exponential while on standby, and the screen time graph in your settings is a function of the hour of day. In computer science, the time an algorithm takes is also a function of input size n. Linear search takes about n steps, binary search about log₂ n steps, and checking every pair of items takes about n² steps. Comparing these functions for large n is exactly why programmers care about the shape of graphs. When n = 1,000,000, log₂ n is only about 20, but n² is a trillion.

Common mistakes: Students often forget that a function must give exactly one output, so they call a circle a function. Another common slip is writing the domain of ln x as x ≥ 0 instead of x > 0, since ln 0 is undefined. Many people also think f(x - 2) moves the graph left, when it moves it right. And many forget to switch the calculator to radian mode. Finally, f⁻¹(x) means the inverse function, not 1/f(x). Those are completely different things.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: find the domain and range of a given function; check whether a function is even, odd or neither; find f(g(x)) and g(f(x)); find the inverse of a one-to-one function; and sketch a graph using transformations. Some universities also ask you to draw piecewise functions and say where they have corners or jumps, which leads directly into the next topics.

Recap: A function is a rule giving exactly one output for each input. The domain is the allowed inputs and the range is the outputs. You met the main families: polynomials, rational functions, exponentials, logarithms, trigonometric functions and their inverses. You learned composition, symmetry and how to shift and stretch graphs. In the next lesson we will ask a sharper question: what value does a function get close to as its input gets close to some number? That question is called a limit, and it is the door into calculus.
key_points: A function gives exactly one output for every input; the vertical line test checks this on a graph.
Domain = allowed inputs, range = produced outputs; watch for division by zero, even roots and logs.
Main families: polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric and inverse functions.
e ≈ 2.71828 is the key base in calculus, and ln x is the log with base e (domain x > 0).
Composition f(g(x)) means feed g's output into f; order matters.
Even: f(-x) = f(x), symmetric about the y axis. Odd: f(-x) = -f(x), symmetric about the origin.
f(x) + c shifts up, f(x - c) shifts right, -f(x) flips, cf(x) stretches.
Always use radians in calculus; f⁻¹ means inverse, not 1/f.
lessons.tip: Draw every new function you meet. A 30 second sketch of the graph will save you from most domain and range mistakes.
lessons.task: On paper, sketch y = x², then y = (x - 2)² + 3, then y = -x² + 4. Mark the lowest or highest point of each and write its domain and range.

lessons.title: Limits
lessons.content:
Imagine you are walking towards the gate of your school. Every step, you cover half of the distance that is left. First you are 8 metres away, then 4, then 2, then 1, then half a metre, and so on. Do you ever touch the gate? In this game, never exactly. But everyone agrees you are getting as close as you like to it. Mathematicians say the limit of your distance is zero. A limit is about where something is heading, not where it actually is. This single idea is the foundation of everything in calculus.

The idea of a limit: We write lim (x→a) f(x) = L and read it as "the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L". It means that when x gets closer and closer to a, from both sides, f(x) gets closer and closer to L. The amazing part is that the value of f at a itself does not matter. f(a) can be different from L, or f(a) might not even exist. The limit only cares about what happens near a, never exactly at a.

A first example with a table: Take f(x) = (x² - 1)/(x - 1). At x = 1 we get 0/0, which is meaningless. So let us try numbers near 1. At x = 0.9, f = 1.9. At x = 0.99, f = 1.99. At x = 1.01, f = 2.01. At x = 1.001, f = 2.001. The outputs are clearly heading to 2. So lim (x→1) f(x) = 2, even though f(1) is undefined. In fact, x² - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1), so for x ≠ 1 the function is just x + 1, which is 2 at x = 1. The graph is the line y = x + 1 with a tiny hole at the point (1, 2).

One-sided limits: Sometimes we approach from only one side. The left-hand limit, written lim (x→a⁻) f(x), uses x values smaller than a. The right-hand limit, lim (x→a⁺) f(x), uses x values bigger than a. The normal two-sided limit exists only if both one-sided limits exist and are equal. Example: let f(x) = 1 for x < 0 and f(x) = 3 for x ≥ 0. As x comes from the left to 0, f stays at 1. From the right, f is 3. Since 1 ≠ 3, the limit at 0 does not exist. The graph has a jump.

When limits fail: A limit can fail to exist in three common ways. First, a jump, like the example above, where left and right disagree. Second, blowing up: lim (x→0) 1/x² keeps growing without bound. We write the limit as ∞ to describe the behaviour, but technically it does not exist as a real number. Third, wild oscillation: sin(1/x) near 0 swings between -1 and 1 infinitely many times and never settles down, so it has no limit at 0.

Limit laws: Limits behave nicely with arithmetic. If lim f = A and lim g = B as x→a, then the limit of f + g is A + B, the limit of f - g is A - B, the limit of f times g is AB, the limit of a constant times f is c times A, and the limit of f/g is A/B as long as B ≠ 0. Also the limit of f raised to a power n is A^n. These laws are why, for polynomials, you can simply plug in: lim (x→2) (x³ + 4x) = 8 + 8 = 16.

Direct substitution: For polynomials, rational functions where the bottom is not zero, roots, exponentials, logs and trig functions inside their domains, the limit at a equals the function value at a. So lim (x→π) cos x = cos π = -1. Always try plugging in first. If you get a normal number, you are done. If you get something like 5/0, the function is blowing up near a. If you get 0/0, that is an indeterminate form, and you need algebra.

Trick 1, factoring: Example: lim (x→3) (x² - 9)/(x - 3). Plugging in gives 0/0. Factor the top: x² - 9 = (x - 3)(x + 3). Cancel (x - 3), which is allowed because x is near 3 but never equal to 3. We get lim (x→3) (x + 3) = 6. Whenever 0/0 appears for a rational function, it means (x - a) is hiding as a factor in both top and bottom.

Trick 2, rationalizing: Example: lim (x→0) (√(x + 4) - 2)/x. Plugging in gives 0/0 again. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate √(x + 4) + 2. The top becomes (x + 4) - 4 = x. So the expression becomes x / (x(√(x + 4) + 2)) = 1/(√(x + 4) + 2). Now plug in x = 0: 1/(2 + 2) = 1/4. The conjugate trick uses (a - b)(a + b) = a² - b² to remove square roots.

The squeeze theorem: Sometimes a function is trapped between two others. If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a, and both g and h have the same limit L at a, then f must also have limit L. It is like a person walking between two police officers; if both officers go to the thana, so does the person. Example: x² sin(1/x). Since sin is between -1 and 1, the expression is between -x² and x². Both of those go to 0 as x→0, so the limit is 0.

The famous limit sin x / x: One of the most important limits in calculus is lim (x→0) sin x / x = 1, with x in radians. Plugging in gives 0/0, but a table convinces you: at x = 0.1, sin x / x ≈ 0.99833; at x = 0.01, ≈ 0.99998. The proof uses the squeeze theorem with a geometric picture of a unit circle. Related results: lim (x→0) (1 - cos x)/x = 0, and lim (x→0) sin(5x)/x = 5, because sin(5x)/x = 5 times sin(5x)/(5x). This limit is the key that later unlocks the derivative of sin x.

Limits at infinity: Now we let x grow without bound. lim (x→∞) 1/x = 0, because 1 divided by a huge number is tiny. For rational functions, divide top and bottom by the highest power of x in the denominator. Example: lim (x→∞) (3x² + 5)/(2x² - x). Divide by x²: (3 + 5/x²)/(2 - 1/x). As x→∞ the small terms vanish, leaving 3/2. Rule of thumb: if the top degree is smaller, the limit is 0; if equal, it is the ratio of leading coefficients; if the top degree is bigger, it goes to ±∞. These limits give horizontal asymptotes.

The number e as a limit: A beautiful limit is lim (n→∞) (1 + 1/n)^n = e ≈ 2.71828. With n = 1 we get 2. With n = 10 we get about 2.5937. With n = 1000 we get about 2.7169. This comes from compound interest: if a bank gave 100% yearly interest compounded more and more often, your 1 taka would approach e taka after one year, never more. Another form is lim (x→0) (1 + x)^(1/x) = e.

Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes: If f(x) grows without bound as x→a from one or both sides, the line x = a is a vertical asymptote. For f(x) = 1/(x - 2): from the right, x - 2 is a tiny positive number, so f→+∞. From the left, it is tiny negative, so f→-∞. To find vertical asymptotes of a rational function, look where the bottom is zero but the top is not, after cancelling common factors.

The formal epsilon-delta definition: Universities usually show the precise definition. lim (x→a) f(x) = L means: for every ε > 0, there is a δ > 0 such that whenever 0 < |x - a| < δ, we have |f(x) - L| < ε. In plain words, however close you want f(x) to be to L (that is ε), I can find a small enough window around a (that is δ) that guarantees it. Example: for f(x) = 2x and limit 6 at a = 3, choose δ = ε/2. Then |2x - 6| = 2|x - 3| < 2δ = ε.

Limits of compositions and a quick strategy: If g(x)→b as x→a and f is continuous at b, then f(g(x))→f(b). For example, lim (x→0) cos(sin x) = cos(0) = 1, because sin x→0 first. Putting everything together, here is a strategy you can use in every exam. Step 1, substitute. Step 2, if you get a number, stop. Step 3, if you get a nonzero number over zero, check signs on each side for ±∞. Step 4, if you get 0/0, try factoring, then conjugates, then known trig limits. Step 5, if x→∞, divide by the highest power. Following these steps in order solves the large majority of textbook limit problems.

Real life example 1, a speedometer: Your bike's speed at exactly one moment is a limit. Suppose in Dhaka traffic you note your position every second. Average speed over a time interval is distance divided by time. Make the interval smaller: 1 second, 0.1 second, 0.01 second. The averages settle to one value, the instantaneous speed. Step 1, pick a time t. Step 2, compute average speed from t to t + h. Step 3, let h→0. That limit is exactly the derivative we study in lesson 4.

Real life example 2, loading bars and algorithms: In computer science, we compare algorithms using limits at infinity. If one algorithm takes n² + 100n steps and another takes n² steps, the ratio (n² + 100n)/n² goes to 1 as n→∞. So for huge inputs they are basically equally fast. This is the idea behind Big-O notation. Also, a download progress bar that adds half of the remaining file each second approaches 100% as a limit, just like walking to the school gate.

Common mistakes: Writing that 0/0 equals 1 or 0 is wrong; it means "do more work". Forgetting that a limit does not care about f(a) is another big one. Students also cancel factors and forget that this only works because x ≠ a. Many say lim (x→0) 1/x = ∞, but the left and right sides go to -∞ and +∞, so the two-sided limit does not exist. And sin x / x → 1 works only in radians.

What exams ask: Evaluate limits by factoring or rationalizing; find left and right limits of piecewise functions and decide if the limit exists; use sin x / x to evaluate trig limits; find horizontal and vertical asymptotes; sometimes prove a simple limit with the epsilon-delta definition. Practise recognising 0/0 quickly and choosing the right trick.

Recap: A limit describes where f(x) is heading as x approaches a value, not what happens at the value. Try direct substitution first. For 0/0, factor, rationalize or use known limits like sin x / x = 1. Two-sided limits need left and right to agree. Limits at infinity give horizontal asymptotes, and infinite limits give vertical ones. Next we use limits to define continuity: when a graph has no gaps or jumps at all.
key_points: lim (x→a) f(x) = L means f(x) gets close to L as x gets close to a; f(a) itself does not matter.
A two-sided limit exists only when the left-hand and right-hand limits exist and are equal.
Try direct substitution first; 0/0 is indeterminate and needs factoring, rationalizing or known limits.
Squeeze theorem: a function trapped between two functions with the same limit has that limit too.
lim (x→0) sin x / x = 1 (radians) and lim (n→∞) (1 + 1/n)^n = e.
Limits at infinity of rational functions depend on comparing degrees and give horizontal asymptotes.
Vertical asymptotes appear where the denominator is zero but the numerator is not.
Epsilon-delta: for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 that keeps f(x) within ε of L.
lessons.tip: When you see 0/0, do not panic. It is not an answer, it is a signal. Ask: can I factor, can I use a conjugate, or is this a known limit?

quiz.explain: Factor to (x - 3)(x + 3), cancel, and get x + 3 = 6.

lessons.title: Continuity
lessons.content:
Think about drawing a graph with a pen. Some graphs you can draw in one smooth go, never lifting the pen from the paper. Others force you to lift the pen: there is a hole, a sudden jump, or the curve shoots off to infinity. Mathematicians call the first kind continuous. This simple picture, "no lifting the pen", is a good starting point, but in calculus we need a precise test that works even for strange functions. That test uses the limits you learned in the last lesson.

Why continuity matters: Many of the best theorems in calculus only work for continuous functions. The Intermediate Value Theorem, the Extreme Value Theorem, the Mean Value Theorem and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus all need continuity. In computer science, continuity is why numerical methods like the bisection method can find roots, why smooth animations look natural, and why small changes in input give small changes in output in many physical simulations. A sensor reading that suddenly jumps usually means something is wrong.

The definition at a point: A function f is continuous at x = a if three things are true. First, f(a) is defined, so the point exists. Second, lim (x→a) f(x) exists, so the left and right limits agree. Third, lim (x→a) f(x) = f(a), so the point sits exactly where the curve is heading. If any one of the three fails, f is discontinuous at a. A short way to remember: "exists, exists, equal".

Checking an example: Let f(x) = x² + 1. Is it continuous at x = 2? f(2) = 5, so it is defined. lim (x→2) (x² + 1) = 5, so the limit exists. They are equal. So yes. Now let g(x) = (x² - 4)/(x - 2) for x ≠ 2, and g(2) = 7. The limit at 2 is 4, since g(x) = x + 2 near 2. But g(2) = 7. Condition three fails, so g is discontinuous at 2, even though it is defined there.

Continuity on an interval: A function is continuous on an open interval (a, b) if it is continuous at every point inside. On a closed interval [a, b] we also need one-sided continuity at the ends: the right-hand limit at a must equal f(a), and the left-hand limit at b must equal f(b). For example, √x is continuous on [0, ∞): at 0 only the right side matters, and lim (x→0⁺) √x = 0 = √0.

Removable discontinuity: This is a single missing or misplaced point. The limit exists, but f(a) is either undefined or wrong. The example (x² - 1)/(x - 1) at x = 1 is removable: the limit is 2, so if we simply define f(1) = 2, the hole is filled and the function becomes continuous. It is called removable because one small fix removes the problem. Graphically it is a hollow circle on an otherwise smooth curve.

Jump discontinuity: Here the left and right limits both exist but are different. The graph jumps from one level to another. A classic example is the floor function ⌊x⌋, the greatest integer less than or equal to x. At x = 2, the left limit is 1 and the right limit is 2. You cannot fix a jump by changing one point. Step functions like this appear in computing all the time, for example integer division, or a price that changes at each kilogram on a courier service.

Infinite discontinuity: The function blows up near a point, usually at a vertical asymptote. f(x) = 1/x at x = 0 and tan x at x = π/2 are examples. At least one side goes to ±∞. These are sometimes called essential together with the next type, but many textbooks list them separately.

Oscillating discontinuity: The function wiggles so fast near a point that no limit exists, like sin(1/x) at x = 0. Even if we define f(0) = 0, nothing makes it continuous there. It is a strange case, but exams sometimes ask you to name it.

Which functions are continuous: Good news: most familiar functions are continuous wherever they are defined. Polynomials are continuous everywhere. Rational functions are continuous everywhere except where the denominator is zero. √x is continuous for x ≥ 0. e^x is continuous everywhere, and ln x for x > 0. sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere, and tan x except at odd multiples of π/2. Also, sums, differences, products and compositions of continuous functions are continuous, and so are quotients where the bottom is not zero.

Fixing a piecewise function: A very common exam problem is "find k so that f is continuous". Let f(x) = kx + 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = x² for x ≥ 2. At x = 2 the right side gives 4. The left limit is 2k + 1. For continuity, 2k + 1 = 4, so k = 3/2. Always check the joining point, because each piece is already continuous on its own.

The Intermediate Value Theorem: If f is continuous on [a, b] and N is any number between f(a) and f(b), then there is at least one c in (a, b) with f(c) = N. In simple words, a continuous function cannot skip values. If you climb from the ground floor to the fifth floor using stairs, you must pass the third floor at some moment. A big use: if f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs, then f has a root between a and b.

Using the IVT to locate roots: Show that x³ + x - 1 = 0 has a root between 0 and 1. Let f(x) = x³ + x - 1. f is a polynomial, so continuous. f(0) = -1 < 0 and f(1) = 1 > 0. By the IVT, there is a c in (0, 1) with f(c) = 0. Note the theorem says a root exists; it does not say where exactly, and it does not say there is only one.

The bisection method: Computers turn the IVT into an algorithm. Take the middle point m = 0.5. f(0.5) = 0.125 + 0.5 - 1 = -0.375, negative. So the root is between 0.5 and 1. Next middle 0.75: f(0.75) ≈ 0.172, positive. Root is between 0.5 and 0.75. Keep halving. Every step cuts the error in half, so after 10 steps the interval is about 1/1000 of the original width. The root is about 0.682. This is the same halving idea as binary search, applied to continuous functions.

The Extreme Value Theorem: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a, b], then f reaches an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum somewhere on that interval. Both conditions matter. f(x) = 1/x on (0, 1] is continuous but the interval is not closed at 0, and the function has no maximum because it keeps growing near 0. We will use this theorem in lesson 11 to find the highest and lowest values of functions.

Continuity of compositions, a worked example: Where is h(x) = √(4 - x²) continuous? The inside, 4 - x², is a polynomial, continuous everywhere. The square root is continuous when its input is zero or positive. So h is continuous wherever 4 - x² ≥ 0, which is -2 ≤ x ≤ 2. At the ends, only one-sided continuity is needed, and it holds. So h is continuous on the closed interval [-2, 2]. Its graph is the top half of a circle with radius 2, and you can draw it without lifting the pen. Another example: k(x) = ln(x² + 1) is continuous everywhere, because x² + 1 is always at least 1, so the log always gets a positive input.

Continuity versus smoothness: Continuous does not mean smooth. The function |x| is continuous at 0: f(0) = 0 and both one-sided limits are 0. But its graph has a sharp corner there. In the next lesson you will see that at such a corner the slope is not defined, so the function is continuous but not differentiable. The rule to remember is one-way: if a function is differentiable at a point, it must be continuous there, but a continuous function can still fail to be differentiable. Keep this in mind, because exam questions love to test the difference with |x| and similar V-shaped graphs.

Real life example 1, the temperature in Dhaka: At 6 am the temperature is 26°C and at 2 pm it is 34°C. Temperature changes continuously; it does not teleport. So by the IVT, at some moment between 6 am and 2 pm it was exactly 30°C, and also exactly 31.7°C, and every value in between. Step 1, the function T(t) is continuous. Step 2, T(6) = 26 and T(14) = 34. Step 3, any N between 26 and 34 is hit. You cannot say when without more data, but you know it happened.

Real life example 2, mobile data and step functions: Many prices are not continuous. A courier like Pathao or Sundarban may charge 60 taka up to 1 kg and 80 taka up to 2 kg. The price function jumps at exactly 1 kg; a parcel of 0.99 kg and one of 1.01 kg differ by a sudden 20 taka. In programming, functions like rounding, integer division and if-else rules usually create jump discontinuities. When you design a fair pricing system or a smooth game control, you often try to remove such jumps.

Common mistakes: Students often check only that f(a) exists and forget to compare it with the limit. Another slip is saying 1/x is discontinuous on its domain; actually it is continuous at every point of its domain, the problem point 0 is simply not in the domain. Applying the IVT without checking continuity is a classic error: f(x) = 1/x has f(-1) = -1 and f(1) = 1 but no root, because it is not continuous on [-1, 1]. Also, the IVT guarantees existence, not uniqueness.

What exams ask: Check continuity at a point using the three conditions; classify a discontinuity as removable, jump or infinite; find constants that make a piecewise function continuous; prove a root exists using the IVT; and sometimes do a few steps of bisection. A tidy table with f(a), the left limit, the right limit and a verdict makes your answer easy to mark.

Recap: Continuity at a point means f(a) exists, the limit exists, and they are equal. Discontinuities come as removable holes, jumps, infinite blow-ups or wild oscillations. Most standard functions are continuous on their domains. The Intermediate Value Theorem says continuous functions do not skip values, which lets us prove roots exist and build the bisection method. The Extreme Value Theorem promises a max and min on closed intervals. Next we use limits to measure the slope of a curve: the derivative.
key_points: f is continuous at a when f(a) exists, lim (x→a) f(x) exists, and the two are equal.
Removable discontinuity: the limit exists but the point is missing or misplaced; redefine one value to fix it.
Jump discontinuity: left and right limits exist but differ (e.g. the floor function at integers).
Infinite discontinuity: the function blows up, as at a vertical asymptote.
Polynomials, exponentials, sin and cos are continuous everywhere; rational, log, root and tan functions on their domains.
For a piecewise function, check continuity at the joining points.
IVT: a continuous function on [a, b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b); opposite signs mean a root.
Extreme Value Theorem: continuous on a closed interval means an absolute max and min exist.
lessons.tip: For every continuity question, write the three checks in a little table: f(a), the left limit, the right limit. Examiners love seeing all three.
lessons.task: Run the bisection method by hand for x² - 2 = 0 on [1, 2] for five steps using a phone calculator. Compare your answer with √2 ≈ 1.4142.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three conditions for continuity at x = a?
quiz.explain: Continuity needs only the value, the limit and their equality; a derivative is not required.

quiz.q: f(x) = (x² - 1)/(x - 1) at x = 1 has which kind of discontinuity?
quiz.explain: The limit is 2 but f(1) is undefined; defining f(1) = 2 fixes it.

quiz.q: For f(x) = kx + 1 (x < 2) and x² (x ≥ 2) to be continuous, k must be:
quiz.explain: 2k + 1 = 4 gives k = 3/2.

quiz.q: f is continuous on [0, 1], f(0) = -2 and f(1) = 3. The IVT guarantees:
quiz.explain: 0 is between -2 and 3, so some c in (0, 1) has f(c) = 0. It does not say how many.

quiz.q: The floor function ⌊x⌋ at x = 3 has:
quiz.explain: The left limit is 2 and the right limit is 3, so it jumps.

lessons.title: The Derivative
lessons.content:
Imagine you are riding a bus from Gabtoli to Motijheel. The trip takes one hour and covers 15 km, so the average speed is 15 km per hour. But that number hides a lot. Sometimes the bus was stuck in a jam at 0 km/h, and sometimes it raced at 40 km/h on a flyover. What if you want the speed at exactly 10:17 am? That instant speed is what the derivative measures. The derivative is the heart of differential calculus: it tells you how fast something is changing at one exact moment.

Average rate of change: Start with something easy. If y = f(x), the average rate of change from x = a to x = b is (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a). This is "change in output divided by change in input". On a graph, it is the slope of the straight line joining the two points, called a secant line. For f(x) = x², from x = 1 to x = 3 the average rate is (9 - 1)/(3 - 1) = 4. If x is time in seconds and f is distance in metres, that is an average speed of 4 metres per second.

From secant to tangent: Now slide the second point closer to the first. From x = 1 to 2: (4 - 1)/1 = 3. From 1 to 1.1: (1.21 - 1)/0.1 = 2.1. From 1 to 1.01: (1.0201 - 1)/0.01 = 2.01. The slopes approach 2. The secant line turns into the tangent line, the line that just touches the curve at x = 1 and points in the same direction as the curve there. Its slope, 2, is the derivative of x² at x = 1.

The limit definition: We write the gap as h, so the second point is a + h. The derivative of f at a is f'(a) = lim (h→0) (f(a + h) - f(a))/h, if this limit exists. This formula is called the first principle or definition of the derivative. Every derivative rule you will learn later is proved from this one limit. When h is tiny, the fraction is a very short average rate, so in the limit it becomes the instant rate.

Worked example, x² from first principles: f(x) = x². Then f(x + h) = x² + 2xh + h². Subtract f(x): 2xh + h². Divide by h: 2x + h. Now let h→0: the answer is 2x. So the derivative of x² is 2x. At x = 1 it is 2, matching our table, and at x = 5 it is 10. Notice how the troublesome 0/0 was removed by cancelling h, exactly like the factoring trick from the limits lesson.

Worked example, 1/x: f(x) = 1/x. f(x + h) - f(x) = 1/(x + h) - 1/x = (x - (x + h))/(x(x + h)) = -h/(x(x + h)). Divide by h: -1/(x(x + h)). Let h→0: -1/x². So the derivative of 1/x is -1/x². It is negative everywhere, which makes sense because the graph of 1/x always goes downhill as you move right on each branch.

Worked example, √x: f(x) = √x. The difference quotient is (√(x + h) - √x)/h. Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate √(x + h) + √x. The top becomes h, so we get 1/(√(x + h) + √x). Let h→0: 1/(2√x). This works for x > 0. At x = 0 the tangent is vertical, so the derivative does not exist there.

Notation: Different books use different symbols for the same thing. f'(x) is Lagrange's notation, read "f prime of x". dy/dx is Leibniz's notation, read "d y d x", and it reminds you that the derivative is a limit of Δy/Δx, a tiny change in y over a tiny change in x. In physics, a dot over a letter means derivative with respect to time. You will also see d/dx (x²) = 2x, where d/dx is like an operator that means "take the derivative of". All of these mean the same derivative.

The derivative as a function: If we compute f'(a) for every a, we get a new function f'(x). For f(x) = x², f'(x) = 2x. The new function tells us the slope at every point. Where f'(x) > 0, the original graph rises. Where f'(x) < 0, it falls. Where f'(x) = 0, it is momentarily flat, like the bottom of a valley or the top of a hill. You can even sketch f' from a picture of f by estimating slopes, which is a favourite exam exercise.

Equation of the tangent line: Once you have the slope, the tangent line at x = a is y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a). Example: tangent to y = x² at x = 3. f(3) = 9 and f'(3) = 6. So y - 9 = 6(x - 3), which is y = 6x - 9. The normal line is perpendicular to the tangent, so its slope is -1/f'(a). Here the normal is y - 9 = -(1/6)(x - 3). Exams often ask for both.

Rates of change in real units: The units of a derivative are output units per input unit. If s(t) is distance in metres and t is time in seconds, s'(t) is velocity in metres per second. The derivative of velocity, acceleration, is in metres per second per second. If C(n) is the cost in taka of producing n shirts, C'(n) is the marginal cost: roughly the extra cost of making one more shirt. If P(t) is a population, P'(t) is the growth rate in people per year.

Differentiability: A function is differentiable at a if f'(a) exists, which needs the limit from the left and from the right to be equal. We sometimes compute the left derivative, using h→0⁻, and the right derivative, using h→0⁺, separately. If they are equal, the derivative exists. If they differ, the graph has a corner. A function is differentiable on an interval if it is differentiable at every point of it.

The |x| example: Take f(x) = |x| at x = 0. The difference quotient is |h|/h. For h > 0 it equals 1, and for h < 0 it equals -1. The right derivative is 1 and the left derivative is -1. They do not match, so |x| is not differentiable at 0, even though it is continuous there. The graph has a sharp V corner, and no single tangent line fits.

Where derivatives fail: There are three common ways. First, a corner or cusp, like |x| at 0. Second, a vertical tangent, like the cube root x^(1/3) at 0, where the slope becomes infinite. Third, any discontinuity: if f jumps or has a hole, it cannot be differentiable there. That last fact is a theorem: differentiable at a implies continuous at a. Proof idea: f(a + h) - f(a) = h times the difference quotient, which goes to 0 times f'(a) = 0, so f(a + h)→f(a).

Worked example, x³: f(x) = x³. Expand (x + h)³ = x³ + 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. Subtract x³ to get 3x²h + 3xh² + h³. Divide by h: 3x² + 3xh + h². Let h→0 and every term containing h disappears, leaving 3x². So d/dx x³ = 3x². Compare with x² giving 2x. Do you see a pattern forming? The power comes down in front and the power drops by one. That pattern is the power rule, which we will state properly in the next lesson.

Worked example, sin x: This one uses the famous limits from lesson 2. Using the identity sin(x + h) = sin x cos h + cos x sin h, the difference quotient becomes sin x · (cos h - 1)/h + cos x · (sin h)/h. As h→0, (cos h - 1)/h→0 and (sin h)/h→1. So the derivative is sin x · 0 + cos x · 1 = cos x. This is why we insisted on radians: the limit sin h / h = 1 is only true in radians, so d/dx sin x = cos x is only true in radians too.

Worked example, checking a piecewise function: Let f(x) = x² for x ≤ 1 and f(x) = 2x - 1 for x > 1. Is f differentiable at 1? First check continuity: from the left f(1) = 1, from the right 2(1) - 1 = 1, so it is continuous. Next, the left derivative uses x², whose slope at 1 is 2. The right derivative uses the line 2x - 1, whose slope is 2. Both equal 2, so f'(1) = 2 and the two pieces join smoothly. If the line had been 3x - 2, it would still be continuous at 1 but its slope 3 would not match 2, giving a corner.

Real life example 1, a cricket ball: A ball thrown straight up has height s(t) = 20t - 5t² metres after t seconds (taking gravity g ≈ 10 m/s²). Step 1, find velocity: s'(t) = 20 - 10t, which you can confirm from first principles like we did for x². Step 2, at t = 1 the velocity is 10 m/s upward. Step 3, at the highest point the ball stops for an instant, so s'(t) = 0, which gives t = 2 seconds. Step 4, the maximum height is s(2) = 40 - 20 = 20 metres. One derivative answered two questions.

Real life example 2, how AI learns: Machine learning models learn by reducing a loss, a number that measures how wrong the model is. The loss depends on the model's weights. The derivative of the loss with respect to a weight tells you which direction makes the loss go down. If the derivative is positive, decrease the weight a little; if negative, increase it. Repeating this millions of times is called gradient descent. Every time a photo app recognises your face, millions of derivatives were used to train it.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to divide by h, or plugging in h = 0 before cancelling, gives 0/0. Students also confuse the average rate (a secant slope) with the instant rate (a tangent slope). Another mistake is thinking continuous means differentiable; |x| is the counterexample. When writing tangent lines, people sometimes use f'(x) instead of the number f'(a). Finally, in first-principles questions, the examiner wants the limit steps; jumping straight to a formula often loses marks.

What exams ask: Find derivatives from first principles for x², x³, 1/x, √x, sin x; find the equation of a tangent and normal at a point; check differentiability of a piecewise function or |x - a| by comparing left and right derivatives; explain the relationship between continuity and differentiability; and interpret a derivative in context, such as velocity or marginal cost.

Recap: The derivative f'(a) = lim (h→0) (f(a + h) - f(a))/h is the instant rate of change and the slope of the tangent line. It is computed from the limit of secant slopes. The notations f'(x), dy/dx and d/dx all mean the same thing. Differentiability needs matching left and right derivatives, and it implies continuity, but not the other way around. Computing every derivative from the definition is slow, so in the next lesson we learn the rules that make it fast.
key_points: Average rate of change = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a), the slope of a secant line.
The derivative f'(a) = lim (h→0) (f(a + h) - f(a))/h is the instant rate of change and the slope of the tangent.
From first principles: d/dx x² = 2x, d/dx (1/x) = -1/x², d/dx √x = 1/(2√x).
Tangent line: y - f(a) = f'(a)(x - a); the normal has slope -1/f'(a).
Units of f' are output units per input unit (m/s, taka per item, people per year).
Differentiable at a requires the left and right derivatives to be equal.
Differentiable implies continuous, but |x| at 0 is continuous and not differentiable.
Derivatives fail at corners, cusps, vertical tangents and discontinuities.
lessons.tip: Do at least five first-principles derivatives by hand. Once the h-cancelling pattern clicks, the formal definition will never scare you again.
lessons.task: Pick f(x) = x³. On paper compute (f(2 + h) - f(2))/h for h = 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 using a calculator, and guess f'(2). Then check it equals 3 · 2² = 12.

quiz.q: The slope of the secant line from x = 1 to x = 3 for f(x) = x² is:
Which limit defines f'(a)?
quiz.explain: The derivative is the limit of the difference quotient as h→0.

quiz.q: The tangent line to y = x² at x = 3 is:
quiz.explain: Slope f'(3) = 6, point (3, 9): y - 9 = 6(x - 3) gives y = 6x - 9.

quiz.q: Why is |x| not differentiable at 0?
options: Its left derivative is -1 and right derivative is 1
quiz.explain: The one-sided derivatives disagree, so there is a corner.

quiz.q: Which statement is always true?
quiz.explain: Differentiability forces continuity; the reverse fails, e.g. |x|.

lessons.title: Rules of Differentiation
lessons.content:
Imagine you had to cook rice from scratch every single time: plant the paddy, harvest it, husk it, then cook. You would never eat. Thankfully we buy rice from the bazar and just cook it. Computing derivatives from the limit definition is like planting paddy every time. It works, but it is slow. In this lesson we learn the rules of differentiation. Each rule was proved once from the definition, and now we can use it as a ready-made tool. After this lesson, finding the derivative of a messy polynomial will take seconds.

The constant rule: The derivative of a constant is zero. If f(x) = 7, the graph is a flat horizontal line, and a flat line has slope 0 everywhere. So d/dx (7) = 0, d/dx (π) = 0, d/dx (1000) = 0. From the definition: (7 - 7)/h = 0 for every h, so the limit is 0. Remember: a number on its own has no change, so its rate of change is zero.

The power rule: For any real number n, d/dx (x^n) = n x^(n-1). Bring the power down in front, then reduce the power by one. Examples: d/dx x⁵ = 5x⁴. d/dx x = 1, because x = x¹ and 1 · x⁰ = 1. d/dx x^100 = 100x^99. The rule also works for negative and fractional powers, which is where it really saves time. Write 1/x³ as x^(-3); its derivative is -3x^(-4) = -3/x⁴. Write √x as x^(1/2); its derivative is (1/2)x^(-1/2) = 1/(2√x), exactly what we found from first principles.

Rewriting before differentiating: The power rule needs the form x^n, so learn to rewrite. 5/x² becomes 5x^(-2). The cube root of x² becomes x^(2/3). 1/√x becomes x^(-1/2). Then differentiate: d/dx (5x^(-2)) = -10x^(-3) = -10/x³. d/dx x^(2/3) = (2/3)x^(-1/3). Most mistakes with roots and fractions happen because students try to differentiate before rewriting.

The constant multiple rule: d/dx (c · f(x)) = c · f'(x). A constant in front just waits outside. d/dx (4x³) = 4 · 3x² = 12x². d/dx (-x²/2) = -(1/2)(2x) = -x. Think of it like a recipe doubled: if you double every ingredient, the rate of using each ingredient also doubles.

The sum and difference rules: The derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives: d/dx (f + g) = f' + g', and similarly for differences. This lets us handle any polynomial term by term. Example: f(x) = 3x⁴ - 5x² + 7x - 9. f'(x) = 12x³ - 10x + 7. The constant -9 disappears. Practise until you can write such derivatives in one line.

The product rule: Here is where many students go wrong. The derivative of a product is not the product of derivatives. The correct rule is d/dx (f · g) = f' · g + f · g'. In words: derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times derivative of the second. Example: y = x² · sin x. Then y' = 2x sin x + x² cos x. Check with a simple case: y = x · x = x². Product rule: 1 · x + x · 1 = 2x. Correct. The wrong "product of derivatives" would give 1 · 1 = 1, which is clearly false.

Why the product rule looks like that: Think of a rectangle with sides f and g, so its area is f · g. If f grows a little by Δf and g grows by Δg, the area grows by a strip f · Δg, another strip g · Δf, and a tiny corner Δf · Δg. Divide by Δx and let it go to zero. The two strips give f g' + f' g, and the tiny corner vanishes because it is a product of two small things. This picture is a nice way to never forget the rule.

The quotient rule: For a fraction, d/dx (f/g) = (f' g - f g')/g², valid where g ≠ 0. A popular memory phrase: "low d-high minus high d-low, over the square of what's below". Here high is the top f and low is the bottom g. Example: y = (x + 1)/(x - 1). f = x + 1, f' = 1, g = x - 1, g' = 1. y' = (1 · (x - 1) - (x + 1) · 1)/(x - 1)² = -2/(x - 1)². The order of subtraction matters: if you swap it, you get the wrong sign.

When not to use the quotient rule: Sometimes simplifying first is faster. y = (x³ + 2x)/x is just x² + 2 for x ≠ 0, so y' = 2x. And y = 5/x³ is easier as 5x^(-3), giving -15x^(-4). Use the quotient rule when the bottom genuinely contains x in a way you cannot split.

Derivatives of trigonometric functions: These six are a must-memorise list, all in radians. d/dx sin x = cos x. d/dx cos x = -sin x. d/dx tan x = sec² x. d/dx cot x = -cosec² x. d/dx sec x = sec x tan x. d/dx cosec x = -cosec x cot x. A memory trick: every function starting with "co" (cos, cot, cosec) gets a minus sign. You already saw sin x proved from the definition in the last lesson. The tan x result follows from the quotient rule: tan x = sin x / cos x, so the derivative is (cos x · cos x - sin x · (-sin x))/cos² x = (cos² x + sin² x)/cos² x = 1/cos² x = sec² x.

The exponential function: The most famous fact in calculus: d/dx e^x = e^x. The function e^x is its own derivative. At every point, its slope equals its height. This is exactly why e is chosen as the natural base: it is the unique base for which this is true. For other bases, d/dx a^x = a^x ln a. So d/dx 2^x = 2^x ln 2 ≈ 0.693 · 2^x. When a = e, ln e = 1, and the formula reduces to e^x again.

The logarithm: d/dx ln x = 1/x, for x > 0. For other bases, d/dx log_a x = 1/(x ln a). So d/dx log₁₀ x = 1/(x ln 10). It is surprising and beautiful that the derivative of a log is a simple fraction. It also tells you that ln x keeps increasing but more and more slowly, because 1/x gets smaller as x grows. That matches the shape of its graph: rising, but flattening out.

Putting rules together: Real problems combine rules. Example: y = e^x (x² - 3x). Product rule: y' = e^x (x² - 3x) + e^x (2x - 3) = e^x (x² - x - 3). Another: y = (ln x)/x. Quotient rule: y' = ((1/x) · x - ln x · 1)/x² = (1 - ln x)/x². Another: y = 3 sin x - 4 cos x + 2e^x. Sum rule: y' = 3 cos x + 4 sin x + 2e^x. Notice the plus sign on 4 sin x: minus times minus.

A worked table for practice: Try to fill this mentally. x⁶ gives 6x⁵. 1/x gives -1/x². √x gives 1/(2√x). x sin x gives sin x + x cos x. e^x/x gives (x e^x - e^x)/x² = e^x(x - 1)/x². x ln x gives ln x + 1. tan x gives sec² x. If you got all of these, you have the basic toolbox. The only thing missing is functions inside functions, like sin(3x) or e^(x²), which need the chain rule in the next lesson.

Proving the power rule for whole numbers: For a positive whole number n, expand (x + h)^n using the binomial theorem: x^n + n x^(n-1) h + (terms with h² or higher powers). Subtract x^n and divide by h. You get n x^(n-1) plus terms that still contain h. Let h→0 and only n x^(n-1) survives. This is the same pattern you saw for x² and x³. For negative and fractional powers, the proof uses the quotient rule and the chain rule, but the final formula is the same, which is why one rule covers everything.

Higher speed with a product of three: The product rule extends naturally. For three functions, (fgh)' = f'gh + fg'h + fgh'. Each term differentiates one factor and leaves the others alone. Example: y = x e^x sin x. Then y' = e^x sin x + x e^x sin x + x e^x cos x. You can also group two factors first and apply the two-factor rule twice; the answer comes out the same.

Real life example 1, a shop's revenue: A tea stall in Chattogram sells cups of tea. If the price is p taka, the number of cups sold per day is about q(p) = 200 - 4p. Revenue is R(p) = p · q(p) = 200p - 4p². Step 1, differentiate: R'(p) = 200 - 8p. Step 2, at p = 20, R'(20) = 40 > 0, so raising the price a little increases revenue. Step 3, at p = 30, R'(30) = -40 < 0, so raising the price loses money. Step 4, the best price is where R'(p) = 0, which is p = 25 taka. Simple rules, real decision.

Real life example 2, cooling coffee and computer graphics: The temperature of a cooling cup of coffee is often modelled as T(t) = 25 + 60e^(-0.1t) degrees, where t is in minutes. Using the rules (and the chain rule we will learn next, for the -0.1), the cooling rate is T'(t) = -6e^(-0.1t). At t = 0 it cools at 6 degrees per minute; at t = 10 at about 2.2. In computer graphics, curves called Bézier curves are polynomials, and their derivatives give the direction of the curve at each point, which is used to draw smooth fonts and animations on your phone screen.

Common mistakes: The biggest one is (fg)' = f'g'. Wrong! Use the product rule. Second, getting the quotient rule order backwards. Third, writing d/dx e^x = x e^(x-1), which wrongly applies the power rule to an exponential; the power rule needs the variable in the base, not in the exponent. Fourth, forgetting the minus signs on cos, cot and cosec derivatives. Fifth, treating constants like π² or e³ as variables; their derivative is 0.

What exams ask: Differentiate polynomials and expressions with fractional and negative powers; use product and quotient rules on mixed functions; prove the derivative of tan x or sec x using the quotient rule; find slopes of tangents at given points; and find where a derivative equals zero. Show your rewritten form first, because it makes your work easy to follow.

Recap: You now have the core rules: constant, power, constant multiple, sum and difference, product, and quotient. You also know the derivatives of the six trig functions, e^x, a^x, ln x and log_a x. With these you can differentiate most formulas that do not have functions nested inside other functions. Next lesson: the chain rule, which handles exactly those nested functions, plus implicit and logarithmic differentiation.
key_points: Constant rule: d/dx c = 0. Power rule: d/dx x^n = n x^(n-1) for any real n.
Rewrite roots and fractions as powers before differentiating (√x = x^(1/2), 1/x³ = x^(-3)).
Sum, difference and constant multiple rules let you differentiate polynomials term by term.
Product rule: (fg)' = f'g + fg'. Never multiply derivatives.
Quotient rule: (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g²; order of subtraction matters.
Trig: sin→cos, cos→-sin, tan→sec², cot→-cosec², sec→sec tan, cosec→-cosec cot.
d/dx e^x = e^x, d/dx a^x = a^x ln a, d/dx ln x = 1/x, d/dx log_a x = 1/(x ln a).
The power rule does not apply to e^x: the variable is in the exponent, not the base.

lessons.title: Chain Rule, Implicit and Logarithmic Differentiation
lessons.content:
Think about a set of gears in a bicycle. When you turn the pedal once, the big front gear turns once. The chain makes the small back gear turn, say, three times. And the back wheel turns with the back gear. If you want to know how fast the wheel spins compared to your feet, you multiply the ratios along the chain. That is exactly the idea of the chain rule: when one quantity depends on a second, and the second depends on a third, the rates of change multiply. It is the single most used rule in calculus, and the reason modern AI can learn at all.

What the chain rule says: If y = f(u) and u = g(x), then y = f(g(x)) is a composite function, and dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx. In the other notation, (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) · g'(x). In words: differentiate the outside function, leaving the inside alone, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. The Leibniz form looks like fractions cancelling, du on top and bottom, and that is a handy way to remember it, though the du's are not really numbers being cancelled.

First examples: y = (3x + 1)⁵. Outside: something to the fifth. Inside: 3x + 1. Derivative of the outside: 5(3x + 1)⁴. Derivative of the inside: 3. Answer: 15(3x + 1)⁴. Next, y = sin(x²). Outside: sin of something, derivative cos of the same something. Inside: x², derivative 2x. Answer: 2x cos(x²). Next, y = e^(5x). Outside: e to something, its derivative is itself. Inside: 5x, derivative 5. Answer: 5e^(5x). Notice that the inside never changes in the outer derivative; we only multiply by its derivative at the end.

General patterns worth memorising: With the chain rule, every basic formula gets a "times u-prime" version. d/dx u^n = n u^(n-1) u'. d/dx e^u = e^u u'. d/dx ln u = u'/u. d/dx sin u = cos u · u'. d/dx cos u = -sin u · u'. d/dx tan u = sec² u · u'. d/dx √u = u'/(2√u). For instance, d/dx ln(x² + 1) = 2x/(x² + 1), and d/dx √(1 - x²) = -2x/(2√(1 - x²)) = -x/√(1 - x²).

Chains of more than two links: Sometimes there are three or more layers, like y = sin³(4x), which means (sin(4x))³. Peel the onion from outside in. Outermost: something cubed, giving 3 sin²(4x). Middle: sin of something, giving cos(4x). Innermost: 4x, giving 4. Multiply all: y' = 12 sin²(4x) cos(4x). Another: y = e^(cos(2x)). Outside e^(...) gives e^(cos 2x); middle cos(...) gives -sin(2x); inside 2x gives 2. Answer: -2 sin(2x) e^(cos 2x). Write the layers down if you get confused.

Combining with product and quotient rules: Real problems mix rules. y = x² e^(3x). Product rule first: (x²)' e^(3x) + x² (e^(3x))'. The second derivative needs the chain rule: 3e^(3x). So y' = 2x e^(3x) + 3x² e^(3x) = x e^(3x)(2 + 3x). Another: y = sin(x)/(1 + x²)³. Quotient rule, with the chain rule for the bottom: derivative of (1 + x²)³ is 3(1 + x²)² · 2x. Take it slowly and label each part.

Proving a^x with the chain rule: Since a = e^(ln a), we have a^x = e^(x ln a). By the chain rule, d/dx e^(x ln a) = e^(x ln a) · ln a = a^x ln a. This is the formula we used in the last lesson, now with a reason. The same trick, rewriting with e and ln, is a powerful general idea.

Implicit differentiation, the idea: So far y was given directly as a formula in x, like y = x² + 1. That is called explicit. But sometimes x and y are tangled in one equation, like the circle x² + y² = 25. You could solve for y, but you would get ± square roots and messy work. Instead, treat y as an unknown function of x and differentiate both sides with respect to x. Whenever you differentiate something with y, the chain rule adds a factor dy/dx. Then solve for dy/dx.

Implicit example, the circle: x² + y² = 25. Differentiate: 2x + 2y · dy/dx = 0. Solve: dy/dx = -x/y. At the point (3, 4), the slope is -3/4. Check with geometry: the radius from the origin to (3, 4) has slope 4/3, and a tangent to a circle is perpendicular to its radius, so its slope should be -3/4. It matches. Notice the answer contains both x and y, which is normal for implicit differentiation.

A harder implicit example: x³ + y³ = 6xy, a curve called the folium of Descartes. Differentiate both sides: 3x² + 3y² y' = 6y + 6x y'. The right side needed the product rule on xy. Collect the y' terms: 3y² y' - 6x y' = 6y - 3x². Factor: y'(3y² - 6x) = 6y - 3x². So y' = (6y - 3x²)/(3y² - 6x) = (2y - x²)/(y² - 2x). At the point (3, 3), which lies on the curve because 27 + 27 = 54 = 6 · 9, the slope is (6 - 9)/(9 - 6) = -1.

Derivatives of inverse trigonometric functions: Implicit differentiation proves these. Let y = sin⁻¹ x, so sin y = x with y between -π/2 and π/2. Differentiate: cos y · y' = 1, so y' = 1/cos y. Since cos y ≥ 0 in that range, cos y = √(1 - sin² y) = √(1 - x²). So d/dx sin⁻¹ x = 1/√(1 - x²). Similarly, d/dx cos⁻¹ x = -1/√(1 - x²), d/dx tan⁻¹ x = 1/(1 + x²), d/dx cot⁻¹ x = -1/(1 + x²), d/dx sec⁻¹ x = 1/(|x|√(x² - 1)), and d/dx cosec⁻¹ x = -1/(|x|√(x² - 1)). The tan⁻¹ one is the most used, for example in integration later.

Logarithmic differentiation, the idea: Some functions are horrible to differentiate directly, like y = x^x, where the variable is both base and exponent, or a long product and quotient like y = (x + 1)³(x - 2)⁵/(x² + 4)². The trick: take ln of both sides first. Logs turn powers into multiplication and products into sums, which are much easier. Then differentiate implicitly, using d/dx ln y = y'/y, and finally multiply by y.

Logarithmic example, x^x: y = x^x for x > 0. Take ln: ln y = x ln x. Differentiate: y'/y = ln x + x · (1/x) = ln x + 1. Multiply by y: y' = x^x (ln x + 1). Neither the power rule (which needs a constant exponent) nor the exponential rule (which needs a constant base) works here, which is why this trick exists. For the long product example, ln y = 3 ln(x + 1) + 5 ln(x - 2) - 2 ln(x² + 4), so y'/y = 3/(x + 1) + 5/(x - 2) - 4x/(x² + 4), and y' is y times that.

Parametric differentiation: Sometimes both x and y depend on a third variable t, often time, like a point moving along a path: x = f(t), y = g(t). Then dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), as long as dx/dt ≠ 0. Example: x = cos t, y = sin t traces the unit circle. dy/dx = cos t / (-sin t) = -cot t. At t = π/4, the slope is -1. Another example: x = t², y = t³. dy/dx = 3t²/(2t) = 3t/2. Parametric curves are how games and animation software describe the motion of objects over time.

A "show that" example: Exams often say: if y = e^(2x) sin x, show that y'' - 4y' + 5y = 0. We only need first derivatives here to set things up, and the second derivative comes in the next lesson, but the idea is the same: differentiate carefully with the chain and product rules, then substitute. Here y' = 2e^(2x) sin x + e^(2x) cos x. Differentiating again gives y'' = 3e^(2x) sin x + 4e^(2x) cos x. Then y'' - 4y' + 5y = e^(2x)[(3 - 8 + 5) sin x + (4 - 4) cos x] = 0. Such questions reward neat, labelled work more than speed.

Differentiating one function with respect to another: Sometimes the question asks for the derivative of f(x) with respect to g(x), for example, the derivative of sin x with respect to x². Treat it like a parametric problem with x as the parameter: d(sin x)/d(x²) = (d sin x/dx)/(d x²/dx) = cos x/(2x). This appears regularly in Bangladeshi university question papers and is easy marks once you see the trick.

Real life example 1, a growing circle of water: Drop a stone in a still pond at Ramna Park. A circular ripple spreads with radius r(t) = 2t cm after t seconds. Its area is A = πr². How fast is the area growing at t = 3? Step 1, chain rule: dA/dt = dA/dr · dr/dt = 2πr · 2. Step 2, at t = 3, r = 6, so dA/dt = 2π · 6 · 2 = 24π, about 75.4 square cm per second. Step 3, notice the area grows faster and faster even though the radius grows at a steady rate, because the outer ring is longer each second.

Real life example 2, backpropagation in neural networks: A neural network is a long chain of functions: input goes through layer 1, then layer 2, and so on, until a final loss number comes out. To train it, we need the derivative of the loss with respect to every weight, even those deep inside. The algorithm that does this is called backpropagation, and it is nothing more than the chain rule applied layer by layer from the output back to the input, multiplying the local derivatives. The chain rule you just learned is literally what trains the AI models used every day.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to multiply by the inside derivative is the number one error: d/dx sin(3x) is 3 cos(3x), not cos(3x). Second, changing the inside when differentiating the outside: d/dx (x² + 1)⁵ is 5(x² + 1)⁴ · 2x, not 5(2x)⁴. Third, in implicit problems, forgetting the dy/dx factor when differentiating y² or sin y. Fourth, applying the power rule to x^x. Fifth, in parametric problems, dividing dx/dt by dy/dt instead of the other way round.

What exams ask: Differentiate composite functions with two or three layers; find dy/dx implicitly and the slope or tangent at a given point; derive the formula for d/dx sin⁻¹ x or tan⁻¹ x; use logarithmic differentiation for x^x, (sin x)^x or long products; and find dy/dx for parametric curves. A classic BUET-style question is to show that a given y satisfies some relation involving dy/dx, which needs careful chain rule work.

Recap: The chain rule says derivatives multiply along a chain: (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) g'(x). Peel layers from the outside in. Implicit differentiation handles equations where y is tangled with x, by differentiating both sides and remembering the factor dy/dx. It also gives the derivatives of inverse trig functions. Logarithmic differentiation turns powers and products into sums. Parametric curves use dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Next we go further: differentiating again and again, to get second, third and nth derivatives.
key_points: Chain rule: (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) · g'(x), or dy/dx = dy/du · du/dx.
Peel layers from the outside in and multiply all the derivatives.
With the chain rule: (e^u)' = e^u u', (ln u)' = u'/u, (sin u)' = cos u · u', (u^n)' = n u^(n-1) u'.
Implicit differentiation: differentiate both sides, add dy/dx whenever you differentiate y, then solve.
d/dx sin⁻¹ x = 1/√(1 - x²), d/dx cos⁻¹ x = -1/√(1 - x²), d/dx tan⁻¹ x = 1/(1 + x²).
Logarithmic differentiation: take ln first; d/dx x^x = x^x (ln x + 1).
Parametric: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt).
Backpropagation in neural networks is the chain rule applied layer by layer.

lessons.title: Higher-Order Derivatives and Leibniz Theorem
lessons.content:
Imagine you are on a bus on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway. Your position changes, so you have a speed. But your speed also changes: the driver presses the accelerator, then brakes behind a truck. The rate at which your speed changes is called acceleration. And when the driver slams the brakes suddenly, your body jerks forward; that sudden change in acceleration even has a name in physics, jerk. Each of these is a derivative of the previous one. In this lesson we take derivatives of derivatives, again and again, and learn to find the nth derivative of a function in one formula.

Second and higher derivatives: If y = f(x), the first derivative is f'(x) or dy/dx. Differentiate it again to get the second derivative, written f''(x), d²y/dx², or y₂. Again gives the third derivative f'''(x), d³y/dx³ or y₃. In general the nth derivative is written f⁽ⁿ⁾(x), dⁿy/dxⁿ or yₙ. Many Bangladeshi textbooks use the yₙ notation, so get used to it. Note the d²y/dx² notation: the 2 on d is on top, but on x it is on the right, because it means "differentiate with respect to x, twice".

A first example: y = x⁴ - 3x³ + 2x. y₁ = 4x³ - 9x² + 2. y₂ = 12x² - 18x. y₃ = 24x - 18. y₄ = 24. y₅ = 0, and every derivative after that is 0 as well. In general, a polynomial of degree m has a constant mth derivative and all derivatives beyond the mth are zero. This is a quick check in exams: if you are asked for the 7th derivative of a degree 5 polynomial, the answer is immediately 0.

What the second derivative means: The first derivative tells you the slope. The second derivative tells you how the slope is changing, which is the bending, or concavity, of the graph. If f''(x) > 0, the slope is increasing and the curve bends upward like a cup, called concave up. If f''(x) < 0, the curve bends downward like a cap, called concave down. For motion, if s(t) is position, s'(t) is velocity and s''(t) is acceleration. For s(t) = 20t - 5t², s'' = -10, the constant downward acceleration of gravity in our simplified model. We will use concavity heavily in lesson 11.

Exponentials: For y = e^(ax), each differentiation brings out a factor a. y₁ = a e^(ax), y₂ = a² e^(ax), and so on, so yₙ = aⁿ e^(ax). For example, the 10th derivative of e^(2x) is 2¹⁰ e^(2x) = 1024 e^(2x). For y = a^x, which is e^(x ln a), we get yₙ = (ln a)ⁿ a^x.

Powers of a linear expression: For y = (ax + b)^m, we get y₁ = m a (ax + b)^(m-1), y₂ = m(m - 1) a² (ax + b)^(m-2), and in general yₙ = m(m - 1)(m - 2)...(m - n + 1) aⁿ (ax + b)^(m-n). If m is a positive whole number and n = m, this becomes m! aᵐ, a constant. Check with (2x + 1)³: the third derivative should be 3! · 2³ = 48. Indeed y₁ = 6(2x + 1)², y₂ = 24(2x + 1), y₃ = 48.

The reciprocal: For y = 1/(ax + b) = (ax + b)^(-1), using the formula with m = -1: the factors are (-1)(-2)(-3)...(-n) = (-1)ⁿ n!. So yₙ = (-1)ⁿ n! aⁿ/(ax + b)^(n+1). Check n = 1: -a/(ax + b)², correct. For 1/x this gives (-1)ⁿ n!/x^(n+1). This result is extremely useful together with partial fractions, as we will see below.

Logarithm: For y = ln(ax + b), the first derivative is a/(ax + b), which is a times the reciprocal. Now use the reciprocal formula for the remaining n - 1 derivatives: yₙ = (-1)^(n-1) (n - 1)! aⁿ/(ax + b)ⁿ. Check n = 2: y₂ = -a²/(ax + b)², which matches differentiating a/(ax + b) directly.

Sine and cosine: For y = sin(ax + b): y₁ = a cos(ax + b). The trick is to write cos θ = sin(θ + π/2). So y₁ = a sin(ax + b + π/2). Each derivative multiplies by a and shifts the angle by π/2. So yₙ = aⁿ sin(ax + b + nπ/2). Similarly, for cos(ax + b), yₙ = aⁿ cos(ax + b + nπ/2). Check: the 2nd derivative of sin x is sin(x + π) = -sin x, correct. The 4th derivative brings you back to sin x, since adding 2π changes nothing.

Exponential times sine: For y = e^(ax) sin(bx + c), there is a neat formula. Let r = √(a² + b²) and φ = tan⁻¹(b/a). Then yₙ = rⁿ e^(ax) sin(bx + c + nφ). The same holds with cos in place of sin. The idea is that differentiating once gives e^(ax)(a sin + b cos), and a sin θ + b cos θ = r sin(θ + φ). Example: y = e^x sin x. Here a = b = 1, r = √2, φ = π/4. So yₙ = 2^(n/2) e^x sin(x + nπ/4).

Using partial fractions: Rational functions are handled by splitting them into simple pieces whose nth derivatives you already know. Example: y = 1/(x² - 1). Since x² - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1), we write y = (1/2)[1/(x - 1) - 1/(x + 1)]. Each piece uses the reciprocal formula, so yₙ = ((-1)ⁿ n!/2)[1/(x - 1)^(n+1) - 1/(x + 1)^(n+1)]. Exams love this type, sometimes with three factors. Partial fractions are covered in more detail in lesson 17.

Using trig identities: Products and powers of trig functions can be turned into sums first. Example: y = sin² x = (1 - cos 2x)/2. Then yₙ = -(1/2) · 2ⁿ cos(2x + nπ/2) = -2^(n-1) cos(2x + nπ/2), for n ≥ 1. Another: sin 3x cos x = (1/2)[sin 4x + sin 2x], so its nth derivative is (1/2)[4ⁿ sin(4x + nπ/2) + 2ⁿ sin(2x + nπ/2)].

Leibniz's theorem: This is the product rule for the nth derivative. If y = u · v, then yₙ = C(n,0) uₙ v + C(n,1) u_(n-1) v₁ + C(n,2) u_(n-2) v₂ + ... + C(n,n) u vₙ, where C(n,r) are the binomial coefficients (the numbers in Pascal's triangle). It looks just like the binomial expansion of (u + v)ⁿ, with powers replaced by derivatives. For n = 1 it gives back the ordinary product rule u₁v + uv₁.

Leibniz in action: Find the nth derivative of y = x² e^x. Choose v = x², because its derivatives quickly become zero: v₁ = 2x, v₂ = 2, v₃ = 0. And u = e^x, with every derivative equal to e^x. Leibniz gives yₙ = e^x · x² + n · e^x · 2x + (n(n - 1)/2) · e^x · 2, and all later terms vanish. So yₙ = e^x (x² + 2nx + n(n - 1)). The golden rule: let the polynomial be the factor you differentiate many times, so the series stops early.

The classic exam problem: If y = sin⁻¹ x, show that (1 - x²)y₂ - x y₁ = 0, and then that (1 - x²)y_(n+2) - (2n + 1)x y_(n+1) - n² yₙ = 0. Step 1: y₁ = 1/√(1 - x²), so √(1 - x²) y₁ = 1. Step 2: square to get (1 - x²) y₁² = 1, and differentiate: (1 - x²) 2y₁y₂ - 2x y₁² = 0. Divide by 2y₁: (1 - x²)y₂ - x y₁ = 0. Step 3: differentiate n times using Leibniz. The term (1 - x²)y₂ gives (1 - x²)y_(n+2) - 2nx y_(n+1) - n(n - 1) yₙ. The term x y₁ gives x y_(n+1) + n yₙ. Subtracting, (1 - x²)y_(n+2) - (2n + 1)x y_(n+1) - n² yₙ = 0. Step 4: put x = 0 to get y_(n+2)(0) = n² yₙ(0), which lets you find all derivatives at 0. This feeds directly into Maclaurin series in lesson 9.

Second derivatives in implicit and parametric problems: For the circle x² + y² = 25 we found y' = -x/y. Differentiate again with the quotient rule: y'' = -(y - x y')/y² = -(y + x²/y)/y² = -(x² + y²)/y³ = -25/y³. For the parametric curve x = t², y = t³, dy/dx = 3t/2. The second derivative is d/dx(dy/dx) = [d/dt(3t/2)]/(dx/dt) = (3/2)/(2t) = 3/(4t). A common error is to just differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and stop; you must divide by dx/dt.

Real life example 1, the bus ride: A bus leaves a stop and its position in metres after t seconds is s(t) = t³ - 6t² + 15t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6. Step 1, velocity v = s' = 3t² - 12t + 15. Step 2, acceleration a = s'' = 6t - 12. Step 3, jerk s''' = 6, constant. Step 4, when is acceleration zero? 6t - 12 = 0 gives t = 2 s. Before that the bus is slowing down, and after that it is speeding up again. Step 5, velocity at t = 2 is 12 - 24 + 15 = 3 m/s, the slowest moment. Engineers designing smooth rides for metro rail care about keeping jerk small, because sudden jerk is what makes standing passengers stumble.

Real life example 2, smooth curves in software: Fonts, car body designs and the paths of animated characters use curves called splines. Designers require the pieces to join with matching first and second derivatives, so that not only the direction but also the bending is continuous. Without matching second derivatives, light reflections on a car body or a camera movement in a game look slightly broken. So higher derivatives are not just exam tricks; they measure the smoothness that the human eye notices.

Common mistakes: Writing d²y/dx² as (dy/dx)², which is the square of the first derivative, a completely different thing. Forgetting the aⁿ factor in formulas like sin(ax + b). Using Leibniz with the wrong choice of factors, making the series never stop. Sign errors with (-1)ⁿ. And in parametric second derivatives, forgetting to divide by dx/dt.

What exams ask: Find yₙ for functions like 1/(x² - 5x + 6), e^(2x) cos 3x, sin² x or x³ e^(2x); state and use Leibniz's theorem; prove recurrence relations like the sin⁻¹ x one above, or similar ones for y = e^(m sin⁻¹ x) or y = (sin⁻¹ x)²; and find second derivatives for implicit and parametric curves.

Recap: Higher derivatives measure change of change: velocity, acceleration, jerk, and concavity. Standard nth-derivative formulas exist for e^(ax), (ax + b)^m, 1/(ax + b), ln(ax + b), sin and cos of (ax + b), and e^(ax) sin(bx + c). Partial fractions and trig identities reduce harder functions to these. Leibniz's theorem gives the nth derivative of a product, and with it you can prove recurrence relations. Next we study the Mean Value Theorems, which connect a function's average change to its instant change.
key_points: yₙ, f⁽ⁿ⁾(x) and dⁿy/dxⁿ all mean the nth derivative; a degree m polynomial has zero derivatives beyond the mth.
The second derivative measures bending: f'' > 0 concave up, f'' < 0 concave down; in motion it is acceleration.
nth derivatives: e^(ax) → aⁿ e^(ax); 1/(ax + b) → (-1)ⁿ n! aⁿ/(ax + b)^(n+1).
ln(ax + b) → (-1)^(n-1) (n - 1)! aⁿ/(ax + b)ⁿ; sin(ax + b) → aⁿ sin(ax + b + nπ/2).
e^(ax) sin(bx + c) → rⁿ e^(ax) sin(bx + c + nφ), with r = √(a² + b²), φ = tan⁻¹(b/a).
Use partial fractions and trig identities to reduce harder functions to standard ones.
Leibniz: (uv)ₙ = Σ C(n,r) u_(n-r) v_r; let the polynomial be the factor differentiated many times.
Parametric second derivative: d²y/dx² = [d/dt(dy/dx)]/(dx/dt).
