lessons.title: Indefinite Integrals and Substitution
lessons.content:
Suppose a friend sends you a video of a cricket ball's speed meter, but you missed where the ball started. You know its velocity at every moment and want to know where it is. That is the reverse of what we have been doing. For ten lessons we started with a function and found its rate of change. Now we start with the rate of change and try to find the original function. This reverse process is called antidifferentiation or indefinite integration, and it opens the second half of calculus. If differentiation is breaking an egg, integration is the much harder job of putting it back together.

Antiderivatives: A function F is an antiderivative of f if F'(x) = f(x). For example, F(x) = x² is an antiderivative of f(x) = 2x, because the derivative of x² is 2x. But so is x² + 5, and x² - 100, because constants vanish when we differentiate. By the Mean Value Theorem consequence from lesson 8, any two antiderivatives of the same function on an interval differ only by a constant. So all antiderivatives of 2x are x² + C, where C is any constant.

The indefinite integral and the constant C: We write ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + C, read "the integral of f of x d x". The long S symbol ∫ comes from an old "S" for sum, which will make sense in lesson 18. f(x) is called the integrand, dx says the variable is x, and C is the constant of integration. Never forget the + C in an indefinite integral; it represents a whole family of curves, each one a vertical shift of the others, all with the same slopes at every x.

Checking your answer: Integration has a wonderful built-in check: differentiate your answer, and you should get back the integrand. If you claim ∫ x cos x dx = x sin x + cos x + C, differentiate: sin x + x cos x - sin x = x cos x. Correct. Because differentiation is mechanical and integration is not, this habit catches most mistakes. Use it in every exam if you have time.

The power rule for integrals: Reversing the power rule for derivatives gives ∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for every n except n = -1. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power. Examples: ∫ x³ dx = x⁴/4 + C. ∫ √x dx = ∫ x^(1/2) dx = x^(3/2)/(3/2) = (2/3)x^(3/2) + C. ∫ 1/x² dx = ∫ x^(-2) dx = x^(-1)/(-1) = -1/x + C. ∫ 5 dx = 5x + C. Just like with derivatives, rewrite roots and fractions as powers first.

The special case 1/x: When n = -1 the power rule would divide by zero. Instead, ∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C. The absolute value is there because 1/x is defined for negative x too, and for x < 0 the derivative of ln(-x) is (1/(-x)) · (-1) = 1/x. So ln|x| covers both sides. Forgetting the absolute value is a small but common error.

Linearity: Integrals split over sums and allow constants outside, just like derivatives: ∫ (f + g) dx = ∫ f dx + ∫ g dx and ∫ k f dx = k ∫ f dx. So ∫ (6x² - 4x + 7) dx = 2x³ - 2x² + 7x + C. Only one C is needed at the end. Warning: there is no simple product rule or quotient rule for integrals. ∫ f g dx is generally not (∫ f dx)(∫ g dx). That is why integration needs special techniques.

The basic table of integrals: Reading the derivative table backwards gives the standard integrals you must memorise. ∫ e^x dx = e^x + C. ∫ aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + C. ∫ sin x dx = -cos x + C. ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C. ∫ sec² x dx = tan x + C. ∫ cosec² x dx = -cot x + C. ∫ sec x tan x dx = sec x + C. ∫ cosec x cot x dx = -cosec x + C. ∫ 1/√(1 - x²) dx = sin⁻¹ x + C. ∫ 1/(1 + x²) dx = tan⁻¹ x + C. Notice the signs: sin integrates to minus cos, because cos differentiates to minus sin.

More standard forms with a: These are used all the time. ∫ 1/(a² + x²) dx = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C. ∫ 1/√(a² - x²) dx = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. ∫ 1/(x² - a²) dx = (1/(2a)) ln|(x - a)/(x + a)| + C. ∫ 1/(a² - x²) dx = (1/(2a)) ln|(a + x)/(a - x)| + C. ∫ 1/√(x² + a²) dx = ln|x + √(x² + a²)| + C. ∫ 1/√(x² - a²) dx = ln|x + √(x² - a²)| + C. You can check each by differentiating. They come up whenever a quadratic appears in a denominator.

Initial conditions: If extra information pins down one point, we can find C. Example: f'(x) = 3x² + 2 and f(1) = 5. Integrate: f(x) = x³ + 2x + C. Use the condition: 1 + 2 + C = 5, so C = 2. Thus f(x) = x³ + 2x + 2. This is the simplest example of a differential equation with an initial condition, a topic we study properly in lessons 22 to 25. Physics problems are full of these: knowing acceleration and the starting velocity and position, you can find the motion.

The substitution method, the idea: Substitution reverses the chain rule. If the integrand looks like f(g(x)) · g'(x), set u = g(x), so du = g'(x) dx, and the integral becomes ∫ f(u) du, which is often easy. Then put back u = g(x). The skill is spotting an inside function whose derivative also appears, maybe up to a constant factor. Write du = g'(x) dx carefully, and make sure no x is left over after substituting.

Substitution examples: ∫ 2x(x² + 1)⁵ dx. Let u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx. The integral is ∫ u⁵ du = u⁶/6 + C = (x² + 1)⁶/6 + C. Next, ∫ x e^(x²) dx. Let u = x², du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2. We get (1/2) ∫ eᵘ du = (1/2) e^(x²) + C. Next, ∫ sin x cos x dx. Let u = sin x, du = cos x dx: ∫ u du = sin² x / 2 + C. Next, ∫ dx/(x ln x). Let u = ln x, du = dx/x: ∫ du/u = ln|ln x| + C. Each time, the derivative of the inside was sitting right there.

The f'/f pattern: A special case worth memorising: ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C, since with u = f(x) it becomes ∫ du/u. Examples: ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx = ln(x² + 1) + C. ∫ tan x dx = ∫ sin x / cos x dx = -ln|cos x| + C = ln|sec x| + C, because the top is minus the derivative of the bottom. Similarly ∫ cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C. And a clever one: ∫ sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C, found by multiplying top and bottom by (sec x + tan x).

Linear substitutions: When the inside is ax + b, the substitution is so simple that you can do it mentally: ∫ f(ax + b) dx = (1/a) F(ax + b) + C, where F is an antiderivative of f. So ∫ (3x + 2)⁴ dx = (3x + 2)⁵/15 + C. ∫ e^(5x) dx = e^(5x)/5 + C. ∫ cos(2x) dx = sin(2x)/2 + C. ∫ 1/(4x - 1) dx = (1/4) ln|4x - 1| + C. Remember to divide by a, the coefficient of x.

Using identities before integrating: Some integrands need rewriting. ∫ sin² x dx uses sin² x = (1 - cos 2x)/2, giving x/2 - sin(2x)/4 + C. ∫ cos² x dx = x/2 + sin(2x)/4 + C. ∫ tan² x dx uses tan² x = sec² x - 1, giving tan x - x + C. And completing the square turns ∫ dx/(x² + 4x + 13) into ∫ dx/((x + 2)² + 9) = (1/3) tan⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + C, using the a² + x² formula with a = 3.

Real life example 1, from velocity back to position: A ball is thrown up at 20 m/s, and gravity gives acceleration a(t) = -10 m/s² (our usual simplified value). Step 1, integrate acceleration: v(t) = -10t + C₁. Since v(0) = 20, C₁ = 20, so v(t) = 20 - 10t. Step 2, integrate velocity: s(t) = 20t - 5t² + C₂. If it starts from height 0, C₂ = 0. Step 3, this is exactly the formula s(t) = 20t - 5t² we differentiated in lesson 4. Integration recovered it from the acceleration alone plus two starting facts. Physics engines in video games do this kind of step, numerically, for every moving object many times per second.

Real life example 2, from marginal cost to total cost: A small garment workshop in Narayanganj finds that the marginal cost of making the x-th shirt is C'(x) = 200 - 0.2x taka (it gets slightly cheaper as workers get faster), and the fixed cost is 5000 taka. Step 1, integrate: C(x) = 200x - 0.1x² + K. Step 2, at x = 0 the cost is the fixed cost, so K = 5000. Step 3, the cost of 300 shirts is 200(300) - 0.1(90000) + 5000 = 60000 - 9000 + 5000 = 56000 taka. Economists and businesses use this reverse step constantly.

Common mistakes: Forgetting + C. Using the power rule on 1/x, or on e^x, which gives nonsense. Writing ∫ sin x dx = cos x instead of -cos x. Integrating a product by multiplying separate integrals. In substitution, leaving some x behind or forgetting to adjust for a constant factor, like the 1/2 in ∫ x e^(x²) dx. Forgetting to put back the original variable at the end. Dropping the absolute value in ln|x|.

What exams ask: Evaluate integrals using the table and linearity; find f given f' or f'' and initial conditions; use substitution for integrals like ∫ x√(1 + x²) dx, ∫ sin⁵ x cos x dx, ∫ e^(tan x) sec² x dx, ∫ dx/(1 + eˣ); use f'/f; complete the square for 1/(ax² + bx + c); and derive standard results like ∫ tan x dx or ∫ sec x dx.

Recap: An antiderivative undoes a derivative, and the indefinite integral ∫ f dx = F + C collects all of them. Learn the basic table: powers (n ≠ -1), 1/x giving ln|x|, exponentials, trig, inverse trig and the a² ± x² forms. Integrals are linear but have no simple product rule. Substitution reverses the chain rule: spot an inside function whose derivative is also present. Always check by differentiating. Next we learn integration by parts, the reverse of the product rule.
key_points: F is an antiderivative of f if F' = f; all antiderivatives are F + C.
Always add + C to an indefinite integral and check by differentiating.
∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C (n ≠ -1); ∫ dx/x = ln|x| + C.
Table: ∫ e^x = e^x, ∫ sin x = -cos x, ∫ cos x = sin x, ∫ sec² x = tan x, ∫ 1/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹ x.
∫ 1/(a² + x²) dx = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C; ∫ 1/√(a² - x²) dx = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C.
Integrals are linear, but there is no simple product or quotient rule.
Substitution reverses the chain rule: u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx.
∫ f'/f dx = ln|f| + C, giving ∫ tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C.
lessons.tip: Keep a running list of every integral you meet, sorted by type (power, trig, f'/f, inverse trig). By the exam, recognising the type will be faster than any calculation.

lessons.title: Integration by Parts
lessons.content:
Think of two friends sharing a plate of fuchka. One is great at eating, the other is great at making more. If they swap jobs at the right moment, the plate gets finished faster. Integration by parts works in a similar spirit. When the integrand is a product of two different kinds of function, like x times e^x, substitution usually does not help. Integration by parts lets you shift the work: you differentiate one factor (making it simpler) and integrate the other, trading a hard integral for an easier one. It is the reverse of the product rule, and after substitution it is the most important integration technique.

Where the formula comes from: The product rule says (uv)' = u'v + uv'. Integrate both sides: uv = ∫ u'v dx + ∫ uv' dx. Rearranging gives ∫ u v' dx = uv - ∫ v u' dx. In the shorter differential notation, with dv = v' dx and du = u' dx, this becomes the famous formula ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du. Some people remember it as "ultraviolet minus the integral of voodoo" (u v minus ∫ v du), which is silly but works.

How to use it: Split the integrand into two parts: u, which you will differentiate, and dv, which you will integrate. Then compute du and v, and plug into the formula. The goal is that the new integral ∫ v du is easier than the original. If it is harder, you probably chose u and dv the wrong way round. You do not need a + C when finding v; one constant at the very end is enough.

First example, ∫ x eˣ dx: Choose u = x (it becomes simpler when differentiated) and dv = eˣ dx (easy to integrate). Then du = dx and v = eˣ. The formula gives ∫ x eˣ dx = x eˣ - ∫ eˣ dx = x eˣ - eˣ + C = (x - 1)eˣ + C. Check by differentiating: eˣ + x eˣ - eˣ = x eˣ. Correct. If we had chosen u = eˣ and dv = x dx, we would get v = x²/2 and a new integral ∫ (x²/2) eˣ dx, which is worse.

Second example, ∫ x cos x dx: Take u = x and dv = cos x dx. Then du = dx and v = sin x. So ∫ x cos x dx = x sin x - ∫ sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C. This is the example we checked in the last lesson. Similarly, ∫ x sin x dx = -x cos x + sin x + C, and ∫ x sec² x dx = x tan x - ∫ tan x dx = x tan x - ln|sec x| + C.

The LIATE rule for choosing u: A helpful guide for which factor to call u: choose the one that comes first in the list L, I, A, T, E. L for logarithmic functions (ln x), I for inverse trig functions (tan⁻¹ x, sin⁻¹ x), A for algebraic functions (powers of x, polynomials), T for trigonometric functions (sin, cos), E for exponential functions (eˣ). The idea is that functions early in the list get simpler when differentiated, while those late in the list are easy to integrate. It is a rule of thumb, not a law, but it works for most textbook integrals. Some Bangladeshi books call it the ILATE rule, putting inverse trig before log; either order works in most problems.

Integrating ln x and tan⁻¹ x: These look like single functions, but we can treat them as a product with 1. ∫ ln x dx: let u = ln x, dv = dx. Then du = dx/x and v = x. So ∫ ln x dx = x ln x - ∫ x · (1/x) dx = x ln x - x + C. Similarly, ∫ tan⁻¹ x dx: u = tan⁻¹ x, dv = dx, du = dx/(1 + x²), v = x. So ∫ tan⁻¹ x dx = x tan⁻¹ x - ∫ x/(1 + x²) dx = x tan⁻¹ x - (1/2) ln(1 + x²) + C, where the last step used the f'/f pattern. The same trick gives ∫ sin⁻¹ x dx = x sin⁻¹ x + √(1 - x²) + C.

Repeated integration by parts: Sometimes you need the formula twice or more. ∫ x² eˣ dx: u = x², dv = eˣ dx gives x² eˣ - ∫ 2x eˣ dx. The new integral needs parts again: ∫ 2x eˣ dx = 2(x - 1)eˣ. So the answer is x² eˣ - 2(x - 1)eˣ + C = eˣ(x² - 2x + 2) + C. Each round lowers the power of x by one, until it disappears. For x³ you need three rounds.

The tabular method: When u is a polynomial that eventually differentiates to zero, there is a quick table. Make two columns: on the left, u and its derivatives until you reach 0; on the right, dv and its repeated integrals. Then multiply diagonally, with signs alternating +, -, +, -, and add. Example: ∫ x³ e^(2x) dx. Left: x³, 3x², 6x, 6, 0. Right: e^(2x), e^(2x)/2, e^(2x)/4, e^(2x)/8, e^(2x)/16. Diagonal products: +x³ e^(2x)/2, -3x² e^(2x)/4, +6x e^(2x)/8, -6 e^(2x)/16. Answer: e^(2x)(x³/2 - 3x²/4 + 3x/4 - 3/8) + C. Fast and tidy.

Cyclic integrals, the boomerang trick: For ∫ eˣ sin x dx, differentiating sin never makes it disappear, so the integral seems to go on forever. But watch. Let I = ∫ eˣ sin x dx. Parts with u = sin x, dv = eˣ dx: I = eˣ sin x - ∫ eˣ cos x dx. Parts again with u = cos x: ∫ eˣ cos x dx = eˣ cos x + ∫ eˣ sin x dx = eˣ cos x + I. So I = eˣ sin x - eˣ cos x - I. The original integral came back like a boomerang! Solve: 2I = eˣ(sin x - cos x), so I = eˣ(sin x - cos x)/2 + C. Important: stay consistent, using the exponential as dv both times.

General formulas from the boomerang: Doing the same steps with constants gives two results often used in exams and engineering: ∫ e^(ax) sin bx dx = e^(ax)(a sin bx - b cos bx)/(a² + b²) + C, and ∫ e^(ax) cos bx dx = e^(ax)(a cos bx + b sin bx)/(a² + b²) + C. With a = b = 1 the first one gives eˣ(sin x - cos x)/2, matching the result above. Another boomerang classic is ∫ sec³ x dx = (1/2)(sec x tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|) + C.

A useful shortcut, ∫ eˣ [f(x) + f'(x)] dx: Because the derivative of eˣ f(x) is eˣ f(x) + eˣ f'(x), we get ∫ eˣ [f(x) + f'(x)] dx = eˣ f(x) + C. Spotting this pattern saves a lot of work. Example: ∫ eˣ (1/x - 1/x²) dx. Here f(x) = 1/x and f'(x) = -1/x², so the answer is eˣ/x + C. Another: ∫ eˣ (sin x + cos x) dx = eˣ sin x + C. Examiners love these because they look hard but are one line once you see them.

Reduction formulas: When an integral depends on a whole number n, integration by parts can relate it to the same integral with a smaller n. Let Iₙ = ∫ xⁿ eˣ dx. Parts with u = xⁿ gives Iₙ = xⁿ eˣ - n Iₙ₋₁. Starting from I₀ = eˣ, you can climb up: I₁ = x eˣ - eˣ, I₂ = x² eˣ - 2I₁, and so on. For powers of sine, a similar argument gives ∫ sinⁿ x dx = -sinⁿ⁻¹ x cos x / n + ((n - 1)/n) ∫ sinⁿ⁻² x dx, and there is a matching formula for cosⁿ x.

A preview of Wallis's formula: When the sine reduction formula is used with limits 0 to π/2 (definite integrals, next lessons), the first term vanishes and we get a beautiful pattern: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sinⁿ x dx = ((n - 1)/n) × ((n - 3)/(n - 2)) × ... ending with × (1/2) × (π/2) if n is even, or × (2/3) × 1 if n is odd. So for n = 4 it is (3/4)(1/2)(π/2) = 3π/16, and for n = 5 it is (4/5)(2/3) = 8/15. The same values hold for cosⁿ x. This result is a favourite in Bangladeshi university exams.

Real life example 1, average waiting time: Suppose requests to a web server, or ride requests on an app, arrive randomly, and the waiting time T until the next one follows an exponential distribution with rate λ per minute. Its average is ∫ from 0 to ∞ of t · λe^(-λt) dt. Step 1, use parts with u = t and dv = λe^(-λt) dt, so v = -e^(-λt). Step 2, the antiderivative is -t e^(-λt) - e^(-λt)/λ. Step 3, evaluating from 0 to ∞ (an improper integral, lesson 19) gives 1/λ. Step 4, so if 2 requests arrive per minute on average, the average wait between them is half a minute. Engineers use exactly this when designing servers and queues.

Real life example 2, sound and signals: Any repeating sound or signal can be built from sine and cosine waves, an idea called a Fourier series, used in MP3 compression, mobile networks and noise cancellation. To find how much of the wave sin(nx) is inside the signal f(x) = x on [-π, π], you compute (1/π) ∫ x sin(nx) dx from -π to π. By parts, ∫ x sin(nx) dx = -x cos(nx)/n + sin(nx)/n², and evaluating gives 2(-1)ⁿ⁺¹/n. So x = 2(sin x - sin 2x/2 + sin 3x/3 - ...) on that interval. Every such coefficient is an integration by parts calculation.

Common mistakes: Choosing u and dv the wrong way, making the integral harder. Sign errors in uv - ∫ v du, especially in repeated or tabular use where the signs must alternate. Forgetting to differentiate u or integrate dv correctly, like writing v = eˣ for dv = e^(2x) dx. In cyclic integrals, switching the choice of u halfway, which just undoes the first step and gives 0 = 0. And forgetting the final + C.

What exams ask: Evaluate ∫ x eˣ, ∫ x² sin x, ∫ ln x, ∫ x ln x, ∫ tan⁻¹ x, ∫ x tan⁻¹ x, ∫ sin⁻¹ x; cyclic integrals like ∫ eˣ cos x or ∫ e^(2x) sin 3x; ∫ eˣ [f + f'] types; derive reduction formulas for ∫ xⁿ eˣ, ∫ sinⁿ x or ∫ cosⁿ x and use them; and apply Wallis's formula to definite integrals from 0 to π/2.

Recap: Integration by parts, ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du, is the reverse of the product rule. Choose u by LIATE so that it simplifies when differentiated. Repeat or use the tabular method for polynomial times exponential or trig. For eˣ times sin or cos, apply parts twice and solve for the original integral. Remember the eˣ[f + f'] shortcut and reduction formulas, which lead to Wallis's formula. Next: more techniques, trigonometric integrals, trigonometric substitution and partial fractions.
key_points: ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du is the reverse of the product rule.
Choose u by LIATE (log, inverse trig, algebraic, trig, exponential) so it simplifies when differentiated.
∫ x eˣ dx = (x - 1)eˣ + C; ∫ ln x dx = x ln x - x + C; ∫ tan⁻¹ x dx = x tan⁻¹ x - (1/2)ln(1 + x²) + C.
Polynomial × eˣ or trig: repeat parts or use the tabular method with alternating signs.
Cyclic integrals: ∫ eˣ sin x dx = eˣ(sin x - cos x)/2 + C, found by solving for the returning integral.
∫ eˣ [f(x) + f'(x)] dx = eˣ f(x) + C.
Reduction formulas: Iₙ = ∫ xⁿ eˣ dx = xⁿ eˣ - n Iₙ₋₁; similar ones for sinⁿ x and cosⁿ x.
Wallis: ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁴ x dx = 3π/16, ∫₀^(π/2) sin⁵ x dx = 8/15.
lessons.tip: Before you start writing, say which part is u and why (using LIATE). If the new integral looks worse after one line, stop and swap your choice; it usually takes ten seconds to notice.

lessons.title: Trigonometric Integrals, Trig Substitution and Partial Fractions
lessons.content:
A good mechanic in a Dholaikhal workshop does not own one giant tool that fixes every engine. He owns a box of small, specialised tools: one spanner for this bolt, another for that nut, a special puller for bearings. Integration is similar. There is no single method that works for every integral. In this lesson we fill your toolbox with three more specialised tools: tricks for powers and products of trigonometric functions, trigonometric substitution for square roots of quadratics, and partial fractions for rational functions. Together with substitution and integration by parts, these cover almost every integral in a first-year course.

Powers of sine and cosine, the odd case: For ∫ sinᵐ x cosⁿ x dx, look for an odd power. If the power of sine is odd, save one sin x for du, turn the remaining even power into cosines using sin² x = 1 - cos² x, and substitute u = cos x. Example: ∫ sin³ x dx = ∫ (1 - cos² x) sin x dx. With u = cos x, du = -sin x dx, this becomes -∫ (1 - u²) du = -u + u³/3 = -cos x + cos³ x/3 + C. If the power of cosine is odd, save one cos x and use u = sin x. Example: ∫ sin² x cos³ x dx = ∫ sin² x (1 - sin² x) cos x dx = sin³ x/3 - sin⁵ x/5 + C.

Powers of sine and cosine, the even case: If both powers are even, use the half-angle identities sin² x = (1 - cos 2x)/2 and cos² x = (1 + cos 2x)/2, which lower the powers. Example: ∫ sin² x cos² x dx. Since sin x cos x = (sin 2x)/2, this is (1/4) ∫ sin² 2x dx = (1/8) ∫ (1 - cos 4x) dx = x/8 - sin(4x)/32 + C. For higher even powers, repeat the identities, or for definite integrals from 0 to π/2, use Wallis's formula from the last lesson.

Products with different angles: Integrals like ∫ sin 3x cos 2x dx use the product-to-sum formulas: sin A cos B = (1/2)[sin(A + B) + sin(A - B)], sin A sin B = (1/2)[cos(A - B) - cos(A + B)], cos A cos B = (1/2)[cos(A - B) + cos(A + B)]. So ∫ sin 3x cos 2x dx = (1/2) ∫ (sin 5x + sin x) dx = -cos 5x/10 - cos x/2 + C. These integrals are the backbone of Fourier series, where you need ∫ from -π to π of sin mx sin nx dx, which equals 0 when m ≠ n and π when m = n (for positive whole numbers).

Powers of tangent and secant: Use tan² x = sec² x - 1 and the facts that d(tan x) = sec² x dx and d(sec x) = sec x tan x dx. Example: ∫ tan³ x dx = ∫ tan x (sec² x - 1) dx = ∫ tan x sec² x dx - ∫ tan x dx = tan² x/2 - ln|sec x| + C. Example: ∫ sec⁴ x dx = ∫ (1 + tan² x) sec² x dx = tan x + tan³ x/3 + C, using u = tan x. Odd powers of secant alone, like ∫ sec³ x dx, need integration by parts, as we saw in the last lesson.

Trigonometric substitution, the idea: Square roots like √(a² - x²), √(a² + x²) and √(x² - a²) are hard to integrate directly. The trick is to use a Pythagorean identity to make the square root disappear. For √(a² - x²), put x = a sin θ, so a² - x² = a² cos² θ and the root becomes a cos θ. For √(a² + x²), put x = a tan θ, since 1 + tan² θ = sec² θ, so the root is a sec θ. For √(x² - a²), put x = a sec θ, since sec² θ - 1 = tan² θ, so the root is a tan θ. Draw a right triangle to translate back to x at the end.

Trig substitution example 1, the area of a circle: Find ∫ √(a² - x²) dx. Let x = a sin θ, dx = a cos θ dθ. The integral becomes ∫ a cos θ · a cos θ dθ = a² ∫ cos² θ dθ = (a²/2)(θ + sin θ cos θ) + C. Back to x: θ = sin⁻¹(x/a), sin θ = x/a, cos θ = √(a² - x²)/a. So ∫ √(a² - x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² - x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C. From -a to a this gives (a²/2)(π/2 - (-π/2)) = πa²/2, the area of a half circle. So the full circle has area πa², proved by calculus.

Trig substitution example 2: ∫ dx/(x² √(4 + x²)). Here a = 2, so let x = 2 tan θ, dx = 2 sec² θ dθ, and √(4 + x²) = 2 sec θ. The integral becomes ∫ 2 sec² θ dθ/(4 tan² θ · 2 sec θ) = (1/4) ∫ sec θ/tan² θ dθ = (1/4) ∫ cos θ/sin² θ dθ. With u = sin θ this is -1/(4 sin θ) + C. From the triangle with opposite side x, adjacent side 2 and hypotenuse √(4 + x²), sin θ = x/√(4 + x²). So the answer is -√(4 + x²)/(4x) + C.

Completing the square first: If the quadratic under the root has a middle term, complete the square to reach one of the three standard forms. Example: ∫ dx/√(5 + 4x - x²). Since 5 + 4x - x² = 9 - (x - 2)², with u = x - 2 this is ∫ du/√(9 - u²) = sin⁻¹((x - 2)/3) + C. Many exam integrals are designed so that completing the square leads straight to a formula from the table in lesson 15.

Partial fractions, the idea: A rational function is a polynomial divided by a polynomial. Adding simple fractions gives a complicated one: 1/(x + 1) + 2/(x + 3) = (3x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 3)). Partial fractions run this backwards: split a complicated fraction into simple pieces, each of which integrates to a log or an arctangent. The method works when the fraction is proper, meaning the top degree is less than the bottom degree. If not, first do polynomial long division.

Case 1, distinct linear factors: For (3x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 3)), write it as A/(x + 1) + B/(x + 3). Multiply through: 3x + 5 = A(x + 3) + B(x + 1). Put x = -1: 2 = 2A, so A = 1. Put x = -3: -4 = -2B, so B = 2. Therefore ∫ (3x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 3)) dx = ln|x + 1| + 2 ln|x + 3| + C. Choosing x values that kill terms, sometimes called the cover-up method, is the fastest way to find the constants.

Case 2, repeated linear factors: A factor like (x - 1)² needs two terms: B/(x - 1) + C/(x - 1)². Example: 1/(x(x - 1)²) = A/x + B/(x - 1) + C/(x - 1)². Multiply through: 1 = A(x - 1)² + Bx(x - 1) + Cx. Put x = 0: A = 1. Put x = 1: C = 1. Compare the x² coefficients: 0 = A + B, so B = -1. So the integral is ln|x| - ln|x - 1| - 1/(x - 1) + C. Notice the squared term integrates to a power, not a log.

Case 3, irreducible quadratic factors: A quadratic that cannot be factored over the reals, like x² + 1, gets a numerator of the form Bx + C. Example: 1/(x(x² + 1)) = A/x + (Bx + C)/(x² + 1). Multiply: 1 = A(x² + 1) + (Bx + C)x. Put x = 0: A = 1. Compare x² terms: 0 = A + B, so B = -1. Compare x terms: 0 = C. So the integral is ln|x| - (1/2) ln(x² + 1) + C. When C ≠ 0, the C/(x² + 1) piece gives an arctangent.

Improper fractions: If the top degree is at least the bottom degree, divide first. Example: ∫ x²/(x + 1) dx. Long division gives x²/(x + 1) = x - 1 + 1/(x + 1). Check: (x - 1)(x + 1) + 1 = x². So the integral is x²/2 - x + ln|x + 1| + C. Forgetting this division step and trying partial fractions directly is a common source of confusion.

The universal t = tan(x/2) substitution: For rational functions of sin x and cos x, like ∫ dx/(1 + cos x) or ∫ dx/(2 + sin x), the Weierstrass substitution t = tan(x/2) always works. It gives sin x = 2t/(1 + t²), cos x = (1 - t²)/(1 + t²) and dx = 2 dt/(1 + t²), turning everything into a rational function of t. Example: 1 + cos x = 2/(1 + t²), so ∫ dx/(1 + cos x) = ∫ (2/(1 + t²)) · ((1 + t²)/2) dt = ∫ dt = tan(x/2) + C. It can get messy, so try simpler identities first.

Real life example 1, the logistic growth of a viral video: Suppose the fraction P of students in a university who have seen a viral video grows by the rule dP/dt = kP(1 - P): growth is fast when some have seen it and many have not. To solve it we separate variables (lesson 23) and need ∫ dP/(P(1 - P)). Step 1, partial fractions: 1/(P(1 - P)) = 1/P + 1/(1 - P). Step 2, integrate: ln|P| - ln|1 - P| = ln|P/(1 - P)|. Step 3, setting this equal to kt + C and solving gives the S-shaped logistic curve P = 1/(1 + Ae^(-kt)). This same curve models product adoption, rumours spreading and, in machine learning, the sigmoid function used in logistic regression.

Real life example 2, engineering systems: Electrical and control engineers analyse circuits and feedback systems with the Laplace transform, which turns differential equations into rational functions. To get back to time-domain answers, they split those rational functions with partial fractions, exactly as in this lesson, and each simple piece corresponds to a familiar signal like e^(-2t) or sin(3t). So partial fractions are not only exam material; they are how engineers read the behaviour of circuits in phones, power systems and drones.

Common mistakes: In trig powers, choosing the wrong function to save when both powers are odd (either works, but you must convert the rest consistently). In trig substitution, forgetting to change dx, or not converting back to x with a triangle. In partial fractions, using a single constant over a quadratic factor instead of Bx + C, forgetting the extra term for repeated factors, or skipping long division for improper fractions. Integrating 1/(x - 1)² as ln|x - 1| is another frequent slip; it is -1/(x - 1).

What exams ask: Integrate sinᵐ cosⁿ with odd or even powers; product-to-sum integrals; tanⁿ and secⁿ integrals; derive ∫ √(a² - x²) dx and similar formulas by trig substitution; use completing the square; split and integrate rational functions with distinct, repeated and quadratic factors; and use t = tan(x/2) for integrals like ∫ dx/(3 + 5 cos x).

Recap: Odd powers of sin or cos: save one factor and substitute; even powers: half-angle formulas. Products of different angles: product-to-sum. Tangent and secant powers: tan² = sec² - 1. Square roots of a² ± x² or x² - a²: substitute a sin θ, a tan θ or a sec θ, then use a triangle. Rational functions: divide if improper, then split into partial fractions for linear, repeated and quadratic factors. Next we give integrals a meaning as areas: the definite integral and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
key_points: sinᵐ cosⁿ with an odd power: save one factor and substitute u = cos x or u = sin x.
Both powers even: use sin² x = (1 - cos 2x)/2 and cos² x = (1 + cos 2x)/2.
Products like sin 3x cos 2x: use product-to-sum formulas.
√(a² - x²): x = a sin θ; √(a² + x²): x = a tan θ; √(x² - a²): x = a sec θ; return to x with a triangle.
∫ √(a² - x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² - x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C, which proves the circle area πa².
Partial fractions need a proper fraction; divide first if the top degree is not smaller.
Linear factors give A/(x - a); repeated factors add A/(x - a)²; quadratic factors need (Bx + C)/(x² + bx + c).
t = tan(x/2) turns any rational function of sin x and cos x into a rational function of t.
lessons.tip: Before integrating, spend five seconds classifying: trig powers, root of a quadratic, or rational function? The right tool is usually obvious once you name the type.

lessons.title: The Definite Integral and the Fundamental Theorem
lessons.content:
Your family's electricity meter does not care how much power the fan used at exactly 3 pm. It adds up all the tiny amounts of energy used every second, all month long, and shows a total in kilowatt-hours. That total becomes the bill. Adding up infinitely many tiny pieces to get a whole is the second big idea of calculus, and it is called the definite integral. Amazingly, this "adding up" process turns out to be the reverse of differentiation. That surprising link, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, is one of the greatest discoveries in the history of mathematics.

The area problem: How do we find the area under the curve y = x² from x = 0 to x = 1? There is no formula from school geometry for curved shapes like this. The idea is to cut the region into thin vertical strips, approximate each strip by a rectangle, and add the rectangles. With more and thinner strips, the approximation gets better. In the limit of infinitely many infinitely thin strips, the sum becomes the exact area.

Riemann sums: Divide [a, b] into n equal parts of width Δx = (b - a)/n. In each part choose a sample point xᵢ, often the right end point. The Riemann sum is Σ f(xᵢ) Δx, the total area of the rectangles. For y = x² on [0, 1] with n = 4 and right end points: Δx = 1/4, heights (1/4)², (2/4)², (3/4)², 1². The sum is (1/4)(1/16 + 4/16 + 9/16 + 16/16) = 30/64 = 0.46875. Using left end points gives 14/64 ≈ 0.219. The true area lies between them.

The definite integral as a limit: The definite integral of f from a to b is defined as ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = lim (n→∞) Σ f(xᵢ) Δx, when this limit exists and is the same for all choices of sample points. Here a and b are the lower and upper limits of integration. Now the long S makes sense: it is a stretched "Sum", and dx is the infinitely thin width Δx. Every continuous function on [a, b] is integrable, and so are functions with finitely many jumps.

Computing a limit of sums: For x² on [0, 1] with n right end points, the sum is Σ (i/n)²(1/n) = (1/n³) Σ i² = (1/n³) · n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6. As n→∞, this tends to 2/6 = 1/3. So the exact area is 1/3. This works, but it needed a special summation formula. For most functions, such sums are impossible to evaluate directly. Fortunately, there is a much better way.

The Fundamental Theorem, part 1: Let f be continuous on [a, b], and define a new function by an integral with a variable upper limit: A(x) = ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt, the area from a up to x. Then A is differentiable and A'(x) = f(x). In words: the rate at which area grows is the height of the curve at the moving edge. Intuitively, moving the edge a tiny bit h adds a thin strip of area about f(x) · h, so (A(x + h) - A(x))/h ≈ f(x). So every continuous function has an antiderivative: its own area function.

Using part 1: d/dx of ∫ from 0 to x of sin(t²) dt is sin(x²), even though we cannot write the integral in elementary terms. If the upper limit is a function, use the chain rule: d/dx of ∫ from 0 to x² of cos t dt = cos(x²) · 2x. If both limits vary, d/dx of ∫ from g(x) to h(x) of f(t) dt = f(h(x)) h'(x) - f(g(x)) g'(x). This rule, sometimes called the Leibniz rule for integrals, appears in exams regularly.

The Fundamental Theorem, part 2: If f is continuous on [a, b] and F is any antiderivative of f, then ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). We write F(b) - F(a) as [F(x)] from a to b. This turns the difficult limit of sums into a simple subtraction! Example: ∫ from 0 to 1 of x² dx = [x³/3] from 0 to 1 = 1/3 - 0 = 1/3, the same answer as the long Riemann calculation, in one line. The + C is not needed, because it cancels in F(b) - F(a).

First evaluations: ∫ from 0 to 3 of 2x dx = [x²] from 0 to 3 = 9, the area of a triangle with base 3 and height 6. ∫ from 0 to π of sin x dx = [-cos x] from 0 to π = -cos π + cos 0 = 1 + 1 = 2. So one arch of the sine curve has area exactly 2. ∫ from 1 to e of (1/x) dx = [ln x] from 1 to e = 1 - 0 = 1. ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/(1 + x²) dx = [tan⁻¹ x] from 0 to 1 = π/4.

Properties of definite integrals: Reversing the limits changes the sign: ∫ from b to a of f = -∫ from a to b of f. Equal limits give zero: ∫ from a to a of f = 0. Integrals add over adjacent intervals: ∫ from a to b + ∫ from b to c = ∫ from a to c. Constants come out and integrals split over sums, as before. If f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b], then ∫ f ≥ ∫ g. And if m ≤ f(x) ≤ M, then m(b - a) ≤ ∫ from a to b of f ≤ M(b - a), which gives quick estimates.

Even and odd functions: If f is odd, then ∫ from -a to a of f(x) dx = 0, since the areas on the two sides cancel. For example, ∫ from -2 to 2 of (x³ - 5 sin x) dx = 0 without any calculation. If f is even, ∫ from -a to a of f = 2 ∫ from 0 to a of f. These facts, which we promised in lesson 1, save a lot of time.

The "a - x" property: A powerful property is ∫ from 0 to a of f(x) dx = ∫ from 0 to a of f(a - x) dx, which follows from the substitution u = a - x. Classic example: I = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin x/(sin x + cos x) dx. Replacing x by π/2 - x swaps sin and cos, so I = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x/(cos x + sin x) dx. Adding the two forms: 2I = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of 1 dx = π/2. So I = π/4. Problems like this are very popular in Bangladeshi exams.

Substitution in definite integrals: When substituting, change the limits too, and you never need to return to x. Example: ∫ from 0 to 2 of x(x² + 1)³ dx. Let u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx. When x = 0, u = 1; when x = 2, u = 5. The integral becomes (1/2) ∫ from 1 to 5 of u³ du = (1/2)[u⁴/4] from 1 to 5 = (1/8)(625 - 1) = 78. For integration by parts, use [uv] from a to b - ∫ from a to b of v du.

Signed area versus total area: The definite integral counts area below the x-axis as negative. ∫ from 0 to 2π of sin x dx = 0, because the positive arch and the negative arch cancel. If you want the actual total area between the curve and the axis, split at the zeros and add absolute values: 2 + 2 = 4. In physics, ∫ v(t) dt gives displacement (net change in position), while ∫ |v(t)| dt gives total distance travelled.

Average value and the Mean Value Theorem for integrals: The average value of f on [a, b] is (1/(b - a)) ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx. For sin x on [0, π], it is 2/π ≈ 0.637. If f is continuous, there is some c in [a, b] where f(c) equals this average. Geometrically, there is a rectangle of height f(c) with the same area as the region under the curve.

Definite integrals as limits of sums in exams: Exams often reverse the process: they give a sum and ask for its limit. Example: lim (n→∞) [1/(n + 1) + 1/(n + 2) + ... + 1/(2n)]. Write each term as (1/n) · 1/(1 + r/n) for r = 1 to n. This is a Riemann sum for f(x) = 1/(1 + x) on [0, 1], so the limit is ∫ from 0 to 1 of dx/(1 + x) = ln 2. The trick is to factor out 1/n and spot r/n as x.

Numerical integration: Many integrals, like ∫ e^(-x²) dx, have no elementary antiderivative, so computers approximate them. The trapezoidal rule joins points with straight lines: ∫ ≈ (h/2)[y₀ + 2y₁ + 2y₂ + ... + 2yₙ₋₁ + yₙ], with h = (b - a)/n. Simpson's rule fits parabolas through groups of three points and needs n even: ∫ ≈ (h/3)[y₀ + 4y₁ + 2y₂ + 4y₃ + ... + 4yₙ₋₁ + yₙ]. For ∫ from 0 to 1 of x² dx with n = 2, h = 0.5: trapezoidal gives 0.25(0 + 0.5 + 1) = 0.375, Simpson's gives (0.5/3)(0 + 1 + 1) = 1/3 exactly, since Simpson's rule is exact for polynomials up to degree 3.

Real life example 1, the electricity bill: Suppose a home in Mirpur uses power P(t) kilowatts at time t hours. Step 1, the energy used over a day is E = ∫ from 0 to 24 of P(t) dt kilowatt-hours. Step 2, if a fan of 0.08 kW runs 10 hours, a fridge averages 0.1 kW all day and lights use 0.2 kW for 6 hours, the integral is 0.8 + 2.4 + 1.2 = 4.4 kWh. Step 3, smart meters measure power many times per hour and add small pieces, which is a Riemann sum in action. Step 4, the monthly bill is that total times the tariff rate.

Real life example 2, fitness apps and GPS: A phone's fitness app gets your speed from sensors or GPS at regular moments. To find distance walked, it adds speed × time for each small interval, a numerical integral like the trapezoidal rule. Similarly, in data science, the area under a ROC curve (called AUC) is a definite integral, computed numerically, that measures how good a classifier is. Whenever a computer turns a rate into a total, a definite integral is being estimated.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that the definite integral gives a number, not a function, so no + C. Evaluating F(a) - F(b) instead of F(b) - F(a). Not changing the limits after substitution, or changing them and then going back to x as well. Treating signed area as total area. In FTC part 1, forgetting the chain rule factor when the upper limit is a function of x. Using Simpson's rule with an odd number of strips.

What exams ask: Evaluate definite integrals with all techniques; find a Riemann sum or evaluate an integral as a limit of a sum; use FTC part 1 to differentiate integrals with variable limits; use properties like the even/odd rule and ∫ f(x) = ∫ f(a - x) to evaluate tricky integrals such as ∫ from 0 to π/2 of log sin x dx (which equals -(π/2) log 2) or ∫ from 0 to π of x sin x/(1 + cos² x) dx (which equals π²/4); and apply the trapezoidal and Simpson's rules.

Recap: The definite integral is the limit of Riemann sums and represents signed area. FTC part 1: the derivative of ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt is f(x). FTC part 2: ∫ from a to b of f = F(b) - F(a) for any antiderivative F. Use properties (sign flip, additivity, even/odd, a - x) and change limits when substituting. Numerical rules approximate integrals that have no formula. Next we push the limits to infinity and meet the Gamma and Beta functions.
key_points: A Riemann sum Σ f(xᵢ)Δx approximates area with rectangles; its limit is the definite integral.
FTC part 1: d/dx ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt = f(x); with variable limits use the chain rule.
FTC part 2: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a) for any antiderivative F.
Reversing limits flips the sign; integrals add over adjacent intervals.

lessons.title: Improper Integrals, Gamma and Beta Functions
lessons.content:
Imagine a tap in your bathroom that is leaking, but the leak slows down every minute. In the first minute it drips 10 ml, in the next 5 ml, then 2.5 ml, halving each time. If you wait forever, does the bucket overflow? Surprisingly, no: the total is 10 + 5 + 2.5 + ... = 20 ml, a finite amount, even though the dripping never fully stops. Now imagine a different leak: 10 ml, then 10/2, then 10/3, then 10/4 ml, and so on. This one also slows down, but its total grows without limit. Deciding which "infinite" amounts are finite is exactly what improper integrals do, and two famous functions, Gamma and Beta, come out of them.

What makes an integral improper: The definite integrals of the last lesson had finite limits a and b and a function that stayed bounded. An integral is called improper if either the interval is infinite, like ∫ from 1 to ∞, or the function blows up somewhere in the interval, like 1/√x at x = 0. In both cases the Riemann sum definition does not directly apply, so we define the integral as a limit of ordinary integrals. If the limit is a finite number, the improper integral converges; otherwise it diverges.

Type 1, infinite limits: Define ∫ from a to ∞ of f(x) dx = lim (t→∞) ∫ from a to t of f(x) dx. Example: ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x² dx = lim (t→∞) [-1/x] from 1 to t = lim (1 - 1/t) = 1. So the infinitely long region under 1/x² from 1 onwards has area exactly 1. Example: ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-x) dx = lim [-e^(-x)] from 0 to t = lim (1 - e^(-t)) = 1. Similarly ∫ from -∞ to b uses t→-∞.

A divergent example: ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x dx = lim (t→∞) [ln x] from 1 to t = lim ln t = ∞. It diverges, even though 1/x goes to zero. This surprises many students: the curve 1/x does get close to the axis, but not fast enough. Compare with 1/x², which gets close much faster and gives a finite area. The two leaky taps in the opening are the series versions of these two integrals.

The p-test: For p > 0, ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/xᵖ dx converges if p > 1, with value 1/(p - 1), and diverges if p ≤ 1. Proof: for p ≠ 1, the antiderivative is x^(1-p)/(1 - p), which goes to 0 as x→∞ only if 1 - p < 0. So ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x³ dx = 1/2, ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/√x dx diverges, and ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/x^1.01 dx converges (to 100), just barely. This test is the main reference point for comparisons.

Both ends infinite: For ∫ from -∞ to ∞, split at any convenient point c and require both halves to converge: ∫ from -∞ to c + ∫ from c to ∞. Example: ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of 1/(1 + x²) dx = [tan⁻¹ x] from -∞ to ∞ = π/2 - (-π/2) = π. Careful: you may not just take lim (t→∞) of ∫ from -t to t. For f(x) = x, that symmetric limit is 0, but ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x dx diverges, so ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of x dx diverges.

Type 2, infinite integrands: If f blows up at the left end a, define ∫ from a to b of f = lim (t→a⁺) ∫ from t to b of f. Example: ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/√x dx = lim (t→0⁺) [2√x] from t to 1 = 2 - 0 = 2. So the region under 1/√x from 0 to 1 is infinitely tall but has finite area 2. Example: ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/x dx = lim [ln x] from t to 1 = lim (-ln t) = ∞, divergent. The p-test flips here: ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/xᵖ dx converges if p < 1 and diverges if p ≥ 1.

The hidden trap in the middle: If the bad point is inside the interval, you must split there. Consider ∫ from -1 to 1 of 1/x² dx. A careless student writes [-1/x] from -1 to 1 = -1 - 1 = -2. But the integrand is positive everywhere, so a negative answer is absurd! The problem is that 1/x² blows up at 0. Splitting: ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/x² dx already diverges, so the whole integral diverges. Always check the integrand for vertical asymptotes inside the interval before applying the Fundamental Theorem.

Comparison tests: Often we only need to know whether an integral converges, not its exact value. If 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for x ≥ a, then: if ∫ g converges, so does ∫ f; if ∫ f diverges, so does ∫ g. Example: ∫ from 1 to ∞ of e^(-x²) dx converges, because e^(-x²) ≤ e^(-x) for x ≥ 1 and ∫ e^(-x) converges. Example: ∫ from 1 to ∞ of (2 + sin x)/x dx diverges, because (2 + sin x)/x ≥ 1/x and ∫ 1/x diverges. There is also a limit comparison test: if f/g tends to a positive finite number, both converge or both diverge.

The Gamma function: For n > 0, the Gamma function is defined by the improper integral Γ(n) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x^(n-1) e^(-x) dx. The exponential decays so fast that this converges for every n > 0. First values: Γ(1) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-x) dx = 1. The Gamma function was invented to extend the factorial to non-whole numbers, and it appears in probability, physics and engineering formulas everywhere.

The key property Γ(n + 1) = nΓ(n): Integrate Γ(n + 1) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of xⁿ e^(-x) dx by parts with u = xⁿ and dv = e^(-x) dx. The boundary term [-xⁿ e^(-x)] from 0 to ∞ is 0, and the remaining integral is n ∫ x^(n-1) e^(-x) dx = nΓ(n). Using it repeatedly from Γ(1) = 1: Γ(2) = 1, Γ(3) = 2, Γ(4) = 6, and in general Γ(n + 1) = n! for whole numbers n. So ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x⁴ e^(-x) dx = Γ(5) = 4! = 24, computed in one step instead of four rounds of integration by parts.

Gamma of one half: A famous value is Γ(1/2) = √π. It comes from the Gaussian integral ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of e^(-x²) dx = √π, whose classic proof uses a double integral in polar coordinates (we will see that idea in lesson 21). With the substitution u = x², ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-x²) dx = (1/2)Γ(1/2) = √π/2. Then the recurrence gives Γ(3/2) = (1/2)√π and Γ(5/2) = (3/2)(1/2)√π = 3√π/4.

Using Gamma with substitution: Integrals of the form ∫ from 0 to ∞ of xᵐ e^(-ax) dx become Gamma functions after u = ax. Example: ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x³ e^(-2x) dx. With u = 2x, x = u/2 and dx = du/2: ∫ (u/2)³ e^(-u) du/2 = (1/16)Γ(4) = 6/16 = 3/8. In general, ∫ from 0 to ∞ of xᵐ e^(-ax) dx = Γ(m + 1)/a^(m+1) = m!/a^(m+1) for whole m. This formula is used in probability for the moments of the exponential distribution.

The Beta function: For m, n > 0, the Beta function is B(m, n) = ∫ from 0 to 1 of x^(m-1)(1 - x)^(n-1) dx. It is symmetric: B(m, n) = B(n, m), which you can see with the substitution x→1 - x. Example: ∫ from 0 to 1 of x²(1 - x)³ dx = B(3, 4). Direct expansion gives ∫ (x² - 3x³ + 3x⁴ - x⁵) dx = 1/3 - 3/4 + 3/5 - 1/6 = 1/60. Expanding is fine here, but for powers like 1/2 it is impossible, and that is where Beta shines.

The Beta-Gamma relation: The most useful fact is B(m, n) = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m + n). Check with B(3, 4): Γ(3)Γ(4)/Γ(7) = 2! · 3!/6! = 12/720 = 1/60, matching the direct calculation. Now harder integrals become easy: ∫ from 0 to 1 of √x (1 - x)^(1/2) dx = B(3/2, 3/2) = Γ(3/2)²/Γ(3) = (π/4)/2 = π/8.

The trigonometric form: Substituting x = sin² θ in the Beta integral gives ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin^p θ cos^q θ dθ = Γ((p + 1)/2) Γ((q + 1)/2) / (2Γ((p + q + 2)/2)), for p, q > -1. Example: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin⁴ θ cos² θ dθ. Here p = 4, q = 2, so we get Γ(5/2)Γ(3/2)/(2Γ(4)) = (3√π/4)(√π/2)/(2 · 6) = (3π/8)/12 = π/32. It also works for fractional powers like ∫ from 0 to π/2 of √(sin θ) dθ, where Wallis's formula cannot help.

Real life example 1, a slowing download: A file server starts sending at 5 MB per second, but the speed decays as 5e^(-0.1t) MB/s. Will it ever send an infinite amount of data? Step 1, the total is ∫ from 0 to ∞ of 5e^(-0.1t) dt. Step 2, the antiderivative is -50e^(-0.1t). Step 3, the limit from 0 to ∞ gives 0 - (-50) = 50 MB. Step 4, so no matter how long you wait, at most 50 MB arrive, and after 30 seconds you already have 50(1 - e^(-3)) ≈ 47.5 MB. The same improper integral describes the total amount of a medicine absorbed by the body as its level decays.

Real life example 2, the bell curve: In statistics and data science, the normal distribution, the famous bell curve used for exam marks, heights and measurement errors, has density proportional to e^(-x²/2). For it to be a probability distribution, the total area must be 1, so the formula includes the factor 1/√(2π). That √π comes straight from the Gaussian integral and Γ(1/2) = √π. Gamma and Beta functions also name whole families of distributions used in machine learning, such as the Gamma distribution for waiting times and the Beta distribution for unknown probabilities, like the click rate of an advertisement.

Common mistakes: Treating ∞ like a number and writing things like e^(-∞)·∞ without a limit. Missing an infinite discontinuity inside the interval, as in ∫ from -1 to 1 of 1/x². Using a symmetric limit for ∫ from -∞ to ∞. Thinking that f(x)→0 guarantees convergence (1/x is the counterexample). Writing Γ(n) = n! instead of (n - 1)!. Forgetting the factor 2 in the trigonometric form of the Beta function.

What exams ask: Evaluate or test the convergence of improper integrals of both types; apply the p-test and comparison tests; prove Γ(n + 1) = nΓ(n) and Γ(n + 1) = n!; evaluate Γ(1/2), Γ(5/2), Γ(7/2); prove B(m, n) = B(n, m); use B(m, n) = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m + n); and evaluate integrals like ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x⁶ e^(-3x) dx, ∫ from 0 to 1 of x⁴(1 - x)^(1/2) dx or ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin⁵ θ cos^(7/2) θ dθ using Beta and Gamma.

Recap: Improper integrals have an infinite limit or an infinite integrand, and are defined as limits; they converge if the limit is finite. ∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/xᵖ converges only for p > 1, and ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/xᵖ only for p < 1. Comparison tests decide convergence without exact values. Γ(n) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x^(n-1)e^(-x) dx satisfies Γ(n + 1) = nΓ(n) = n! and Γ(1/2) = √π. B(m, n) = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m + n) and has a handy trigonometric form. Next we use integrals to compute areas, volumes, lengths and more.
key_points: Improper integrals have an infinite limit or an infinite integrand and are defined as limits.
∫ from 1 to ∞ of 1/xᵖ converges iff p > 1 (value 1/(p - 1)); ∫ from 0 to 1 of 1/xᵖ converges iff p < 1.
Always check for infinite discontinuities inside the interval: ∫ from -1 to 1 of 1/x² diverges.
Comparison test: smaller than convergent converges; bigger than divergent diverges.
Γ(n) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x^(n-1) e^(-x) dx; Γ(n + 1) = nΓ(n); Γ(n + 1) = n!; Γ(1/2) = √π.
∫ from 0 to ∞ of xᵐ e^(-ax) dx = Γ(m + 1)/a^(m+1).
B(m, n) = ∫ from 0 to 1 of x^(m-1)(1 - x)^(n-1) dx = Γ(m)Γ(n)/Γ(m + n), and B(m, n) = B(n, m).
∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin^p θ cos^q θ dθ = Γ((p + 1)/2)Γ((q + 1)/2)/(2Γ((p + q + 2)/2)).
lessons.tip: Before using the Fundamental Theorem on any integral, look for two danger signs: an ∞ in the limits, or a denominator that becomes zero inside the interval. If you see either, switch to limit notation.

lessons.title: Applications of Integration
lessons.content:
A potter in Bijoypur, Netrokona, shapes a clay pot on a spinning wheel. As the wheel turns, his hands trace a curved outline, and the spinning turns that flat outline into a round 3D pot. How much water will the pot hold? How much clay does its surface need? How long is the curved rim of a decorative pattern? None of these have school-geometry formulas, because the shapes are curved. But each of them is an integral. In this lesson we use the idea "slice into tiny pieces and add them up" to compute areas between curves, volumes of solids, lengths of curves, surface areas and physical work.

The slicing idea: Every application in this lesson follows one plan. Step 1, cut the object into thin slices of width dx (or dy). Step 2, approximate the quantity for one slice with a simple formula: a rectangle's area, a disk's volume, a tiny straight segment's length. Step 3, add up all the slices with an integral. If you understand this plan, you do not need to memorise many formulas; you can build them yourself.

Area between two curves: If f(x) ≥ g(x) on [a, b], the area between them is A = ∫ from a to b of [f(x) - g(x)] dx. Each thin vertical strip has height (top - bottom) and width dx. Example: the area between y = x and y = x². They meet where x = x², so at x = 0 and x = 1. On [0, 1], x is on top. So A = ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x - x²) dx = 1/2 - 1/3 = 1/6. Another: between y = 2x and y = x², meeting at 0 and 2: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (2x - x²) dx = 4 - 8/3 = 4/3.

When the curves cross: If the curves swap positions inside the interval, split the integral where they cross, and always subtract bottom from top in each piece. For example, the area between y = sin x and y = cos x from 0 to π/2: they cross at π/4. On [0, π/4], cos is on top; on [π/4, π/2], sin is on top. The area is ∫ from 0 to π/4 of (cos x - sin x) dx + ∫ from π/4 to π/2 of (sin x - cos x) dx = (√2 - 1) + (√2 - 1) = 2√2 - 2. A single integral of (cos x - sin x) would wrongly give 0.

Integrating with respect to y: Sometimes horizontal strips are easier, especially when curves are given as x = g(y). Area = ∫ from c to d of [right - left] dy. Example: the region between x = y² and x = y + 2. They meet when y² = y + 2, so y = -1 and y = 2. The right curve is x = y + 2. So A = ∫ from -1 to 2 of (y + 2 - y²) dy = [y²/2 + 2y - y³/3] from -1 to 2 = (2 + 4 - 8/3) - (1/2 - 2 + 1/3) = 10/3 + 7/6 = 9/2. Doing this with vertical strips would need two separate integrals.

Classic areas: The ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 has area 4 ∫ from 0 to a of (b/a)√(a² - x²) dx. Using the circle formula from lesson 17, ∫ from 0 to a of √(a² - x²) dx = πa²/4, so the area is 4(b/a)(πa²/4) = πab. When a = b = r, this is the circle's πr². In polar coordinates, the area swept by r = f(θ) from θ = α to β is (1/2) ∫ from α to β of r² dθ, since each thin wedge is like a triangle with area (1/2)r² dθ. The cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ), a heart-shaped curve, has area 3πa²/2.

Volumes by slicing: If a solid has cross-sectional area A(x) at position x, its volume is V = ∫ from a to b of A(x) dx. Each slice is a thin slab of volume A(x) dx. This is Cavalieri's idea: two solids with the same cross-section areas at every height have the same volume. Example: a pyramid of height h with a square base of side s. At distance x from the top, the square side is s·x/h, so A(x) = s²x²/h². V = ∫ from 0 to h of s²x²/h² dx = s²h/3, the familiar one-third base times height.

Solids of revolution, the disk method: Rotate the region under y = f(x), from a to b, around the x-axis. Each slice becomes a thin disk of radius f(x), with volume π[f(x)]² dx. So V = π ∫ from a to b of [f(x)]² dx. Example: rotate y = √x from 0 to 4: V = π ∫ from 0 to 4 of x dx = 8π. The sphere: rotate y = √(r² - x²) from -r to r: V = π ∫ from -r to r of (r² - x²) dx = π(2r³ - 2r³/3) = 4πr³/3. The cone: rotate y = (r/h)x from 0 to h: V = π ∫ from 0 to h of r²x²/h² dx = πr²h/3. School formulas, now proved.

The washer method: If the region lies between two curves, f(x) on the outside and g(x) on the inside, rotating it makes slices shaped like washers (flat rings). The volume is V = π ∫ from a to b of ([f(x)]² - [g(x)]²) dx. Careful: it is the difference of squares, not the square of the difference. Example: rotate the region between y = x and y = x² (0 ≤ x ≤ 1) about the x-axis. The outer radius is x and the inner is x². V = π ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x² - x⁴) dx = π(1/3 - 1/5) = 2π/15.

The shell method: For rotation around the y-axis, it is often easier to use thin cylindrical shells. A vertical strip at distance x from the axis, with height f(x) and width dx, sweeps out a thin cylinder with volume about 2πx f(x) dx (circumference times height times thickness). So V = 2π ∫ from a to b of x f(x) dx. Example: rotate the region under y = x - x² (0 ≤ x ≤ 1) around the y-axis. V = 2π ∫ from 0 to 1 of x(x - x²) dx = 2π(1/3 - 1/4) = π/6. With disks, you would need to solve y = x - x² for x, which is messy.

Arc length: The length of a curve y = f(x) from a to b is L = ∫ from a to b of √(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx. Reason: a tiny piece of curve is almost a straight segment with horizontal part dx and vertical part dy, so its length is √(dx² + dy²) = √(1 + (dy/dx)²) dx by Pythagoras. Example: y = (2/3)x^(3/2) from 0 to 3. f'(x) = √x, so L = ∫ from 0 to 3 of √(1 + x) dx = (2/3)[(1 + x)^(3/2)] from 0 to 3 = (2/3)(8 - 1) = 14/3. For a parametric curve, L = ∫ √((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) dt. For x = r cos t, y = r sin t from 0 to 2π, this gives ∫ r dt = 2πr, the circumference.

Surface area of revolution: Rotating y = f(x) ≥ 0 around the x-axis creates a surface. Each tiny arc piece of length ds sweeps a thin band of area 2πy ds. So S = 2π ∫ from a to b of f(x)√(1 + [f'(x)]²) dx. Example: the sphere, y = √(r² - x²). Then y' = -x/√(r² - x²), and y√(1 + y'²) simplifies to exactly r. So S = 2π ∫ from -r to r of r dx = 2πr · 2r = 4πr². Archimedes found this result more than 2000 years ago by clever geometry; calculus gets it in two lines.

Work done by a variable force: If a constant force F moves an object a distance d, the work is W = Fd. If the force changes with position, W = ∫ from a to b of F(x) dx. Example: a spring obeys Hooke's law F = kx. With k = 200 N/m, stretching it from 0 to 0.1 m needs W = ∫ from 0 to 0.1 of 200x dx = 100(0.01) = 1 joule. Another classic is pumping water out of a tank: each thin layer of water has to be lifted a different height, so you integrate weight × lift distance over the layers.

Centroids, briefly: The centre of mass (centroid) of a flat region of uniform density, bounded by y = f(x) from a to b, has x̄ = (1/A) ∫ x f(x) dx, where A is the area. For the triangle under y = x from 0 to 1, A = 1/2 and ∫ x · x dx = 1/3, so x̄ = 2/3: the balancing point is two-thirds of the way along, matching the geometry fact that the centroid lies at the intersection of the medians. Engineers use centroids to design beams and to balance machines.

Real life example 1, a paraboloid bowl: A cooking bowl (or a solar cooker dish) has a cross-section shaped like y = x², with x and y in decimetres, and it is 1 dm deep. How much water does it hold when full? Step 1, rotating around the y-axis, at height y the water surface is a disk of radius x = √y. Step 2, slice horizontally: each slice is a disk of area πx² = πy and thickness dy. Step 3, V = ∫ from 0 to 1 of πy dy = π/2 ≈ 1.57 cubic decimetres, which is about 1.57 litres. Step 4, interestingly, this is exactly half of the cylinder with the same top and depth (π · 1 · 1 = π litres).

Real life example 2, medical scans and 3D printing: A CT scanner takes many cross-sectional X-ray images of the body, each a slice a few millimetres thick. To measure the volume of an organ or a tumour, software measures the area of the organ in each slice and adds area × thickness for all slices: exactly the slicing method V ≈ Σ A(xᵢ)Δx. 3D printing software works the same way in reverse: it cuts a design into thin layers and prints them one by one, while CAD programs compute volumes and surface areas with integrals to estimate material and cost.

Common mistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order (bottom minus top) or not splitting where curves cross. Using a single washer formula π(f - g)² instead of π(f² - g²). Mixing up the axis of rotation and using x instead of y. Forgetting the 2πx factor in the shell method. In arc length, forgetting the square root or the 1 inside it. Using degrees instead of radians in polar areas. And forgetting units: area in square units, volume in cubic units.

What exams ask: Find areas between curves, sometimes with respect to y; area of an ellipse or a circle by integration; polar areas such as cardioids or rose curves; volumes of solids of revolution by disk, washer and shell methods, often proving sphere and cone formulas; arc lengths of curves like y = cosh x, y = x^(3/2) or a cycloid; surface areas of spheres and cones; and work done by springs or pumping.

Recap: Slice, approximate, add. Area between curves: ∫ (top - bottom) dx or ∫ (right - left) dy. Volume by cross-sections: ∫ A(x) dx; disks π∫ f²; washers π∫ (f² - g²); shells 2π∫ x f(x) dx. Arc length: ∫ √(1 + f'²) dx. Surface area: 2π∫ f √(1 + f'²) dx. Work: ∫ F(x) dx. These same ideas, with two-dimensional slicing, lead to double and triple integrals, which come next.
key_points: Plan for every application: slice into thin pieces, approximate one piece, add with an integral.
Area between curves: ∫ (top - bottom) dx, or ∫ (right - left) dy; split where curves cross.
Polar area: (1/2) ∫ r² dθ; ellipse area πab; cardioid r = a(1 + cos θ) has area 3πa²/2.
Volume by slicing: ∫ A(x) dx; disks: π∫ f² dx; washers: π∫ (f² - g²) dx.
Shells (rotation about the y-axis): V = 2π∫ x f(x) dx.
Arc length: ∫ √(1 + f'(x)²) dx, or ∫ √(x'² + y'²) dt for parametric curves.
Surface of revolution: S = 2π∫ f √(1 + f'²) dx; it gives the sphere area 4πr².
Work by a variable force: W = ∫ F(x) dx (spring: F = kx).
lessons.tip: Always draw the region and one representative slice before writing an integral. The slice tells you the formula: its height, its radius and its thickness.
lessons.task: Find a bowl or glass at home with a smooth curved profile. Measure its depth and the radius at a few heights with a ruler, then estimate its volume by adding up thin disks (π r² × thickness). Check by filling it with water using a measuring cup.

lessons.title: Multiple Integrals
lessons.content:
After a heavy monsoon night, the rain gauges across a river basin in Sylhet show different readings: 80 mm here, 120 mm there, 60 mm on the hills. Engineers want to know the total volume of water that fell on the whole basin, because it decides whether the rivers will flood tomorrow. The rainfall depth changes from place to place in two directions, east-west and north-south. To add it all up, we need to integrate over an area, not just along a line. That is a double integral. In this lesson we extend integration to two and three dimensions, which lets us compute volumes, masses, averages and probabilities over regions.

From single to double integrals: A single integral adds f(x) dx over an interval: thin strips. A double integral adds f(x, y) dA over a region R in the plane, where dA is a tiny patch of area. Picture the surface z = f(x, y) above R. Divide R into small rectangles of area ΔA, build a thin column on each, of height f(xᵢ, yᵢ), and add the column volumes: Σ f(xᵢ, yᵢ)ΔA. As the rectangles shrink, the sum approaches the double integral ∬_R f(x, y) dA, which equals the volume under the surface when f ≥ 0.

Iterated integrals and Fubini's theorem: We almost never compute double integrals from sums. Instead we integrate one variable at a time. For a rectangle R = [a, b] × [c, d], ∬_R f dA = ∫ from a to b [∫ from c to d f(x, y) dy] dx. The inner integral treats x as a constant, exactly like a partial derivative in reverse. Fubini's theorem says that for continuous f, the order does not matter: you can also integrate x first and y second. It is like counting the seats in a cinema hall row by row or column by column; the total is the same.

A first example: ∬ (x + 2y) dA over R = [0, 2] × [0, 1]. Inner integral in y: ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x + 2y) dy = [xy + y²] from 0 to 1 = x + 1. Outer integral in x: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x + 1) dx = 2 + 2 = 4. Other order: ∫ from 0 to 2 of (x + 2y) dx = 2 + 4y, then ∫ from 0 to 1 of (2 + 4y) dy = 2 + 2 = 4. Same answer, as Fubini promised. If f(x, y) = g(x)h(y) on a rectangle, the double integral even splits into a product: (∫ g dx)(∫ h dy).

Non-rectangular regions: Most regions are not rectangles. A type I region lies between two curves in y: a ≤ x ≤ b and g₁(x) ≤ y ≤ g₂(x). Then ∬_R f dA = ∫ from a to b ∫ from g₁(x) to g₂(x) f(x, y) dy dx. A type II region lies between two curves in x: c ≤ y ≤ d and h₁(y) ≤ x ≤ h₂(y), integrated with x inside. The inner limits may depend on the outer variable, but the outer limits must be constants. Always draw the region first.

Example over a curved region: Integrate f(x, y) = xy over the region between y = x² and y = x. They meet at x = 0 and 1, and y = x is on top. So the integral is ∫ from 0 to 1 ∫ from x² to x of xy dy dx. Inner: x[y²/2] from x² to x = x(x² - x⁴)/2. Outer: (1/2) ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x³ - x⁵) dx = (1/2)(1/4 - 1/6) = 1/24. Setting f = 1 instead gives ∬ 1 dA = ∫ from 0 to 1 of (x - x²) dx = 1/6, the area of the region, matching lesson 20.

Changing the order of integration: Sometimes the inner integral is impossible in one order but easy in the other. Example: ∫ from 0 to 1 ∫ from x to 1 of e^(y²) dy dx. The function e^(y²) has no elementary antiderivative in y, so we are stuck. Draw the region: 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and x ≤ y ≤ 1, a triangle with corners (0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1). Described the other way: 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 and 0 ≤ x ≤ y. Now ∫ from 0 to 1 ∫ from 0 to y of e^(y²) dx dy = ∫ from 0 to 1 of y e^(y²) dy = (e - 1)/2. Changing the order is a favourite exam question, and the sketch is the key step.

Double integrals in polar coordinates: For circles, rings and sectors, polar coordinates are natural. The tiny area element is not dr dθ but r dr dθ, because a small polar patch has sides dr and r dθ. This r is exactly the Jacobian from lesson 14. So ∬_R f dA = ∬ f(r cos θ, r sin θ) r dr dθ. Example: over the disk of radius a, ∬ (x² + y²) dA = ∫ from 0 to 2π ∫ from 0 to a of r² · r dr dθ = 2π · a⁴/4 = πa⁴/2. With f = 1 we get ∫∫ r dr dθ = πa², the disk area.

Volume with polar coordinates: Find the volume under the paraboloid z = 4 - x² - y² and above the xy-plane. The surface meets the plane where x² + y² = 4, a circle of radius 2. In polar form z = 4 - r². V = ∫ from 0 to 2π ∫ from 0 to 2 of (4 - r²) r dr dθ = 2π [2r² - r⁴/4] from 0 to 2 = 2π(8 - 4) = 8π. In Cartesian coordinates this would need square-root limits and trig substitution; polar makes it short.

The Gaussian integral, finally: Lesson 19 promised a proof that ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of e^(-x²) dx = √π. Call it I. Then I² = (∫ e^(-x²) dx)(∫ e^(-y²) dy) = ∬ over the whole plane of e^(-(x² + y²)) dA. In polar coordinates this is ∫ from 0 to 2π ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-r²) r dr dθ. The inner integral is [-e^(-r²)/2] from 0 to ∞ = 1/2, so I² = 2π · 1/2 = π, and I = √π. This beautiful trick, squaring and switching to polar, is one of the most famous calculations in mathematics.

General change of variables: For a substitution x = x(u, v), y = y(u, v), the area element becomes dA = |J| du dv, where J = ∂(x, y)/∂(u, v) is the Jacobian. Example: for the region bounded by the lines x + y = 0, x + y = 2, x - y = 0, x - y = 4, put u = x + y and v = x - y, so the region becomes the rectangle 0 ≤ u ≤ 2, 0 ≤ v ≤ 4. Here x = (u + v)/2 and y = (u - v)/2, so J = (1/2)(-1/2) - (1/2)(1/2) = -1/2 and |J| = 1/2. The area is ∬ (1/2) du dv = (1/2)(2)(4) = 4.

Triple integrals: For a solid region E in space, ∭_E f(x, y, z) dV adds f over tiny boxes of volume dV = dx dy dz. With f = 1 it gives the volume of E. For a box it is three nested integrals with constant limits: ∭ over [0, 1]³ of xyz dV = (1/2)(1/2)(1/2) = 1/8. For curved solids the limits nest: z between two surfaces, then y between two curves, then x between two numbers. Example: the tetrahedron x, y, z ≥ 0, x + y + z ≤ 1 has volume ∫ from 0 to 1 ∫ from 0 to 1-x ∫ from 0 to 1-x-y of dz dy dx = 1/6.

Cylindrical and spherical coordinates: For solids with circular symmetry, use cylindrical coordinates (r, θ, z), where dV = r dr dθ dz, the polar idea plus height. For spheres, use spherical coordinates (ρ, φ, θ): ρ is the distance from the origin, φ the angle down from the positive z-axis, and θ the usual polar angle; then dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ. Example: the volume of a sphere of radius a is ∫ from 0 to 2π ∫ from 0 to π ∫ from 0 to a of ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ = 2π · 2 · a³/3 = 4πa³/3. A third proof of the same school formula!

Physical applications: If a thin plate occupies region R and has density ρ(x, y) per unit area, its mass is ∬_R ρ dA, and the centre of mass has x̄ = (1/M) ∬ x ρ dA and ȳ = (1/M) ∬ y ρ dA. The average value of f over R is (1/Area) ∬_R f dA. In probability, if X and Y have a joint density p(x, y), the probability that (X, Y) lands in a region R is ∬_R p(x, y) dA, and the total over the whole plane must be 1.

Real life example 1, rainfall over a river basin: Suppose rainfall depth (in metres) over a rectangular catchment 10 km by 6 km is modelled as d(x, y) = 0.06 + 0.002x + 0.001y, with x and y in km. Step 1, the volume of rain is ∬ d dA, with area in square metres, so we convert: 1 km² = 10⁶ m². Step 2, ∫ from 0 to 10 ∫ from 0 to 6 of (0.06 + 0.002x + 0.001y) dy dx = ∫ from 0 to 10 of (0.36 + 0.012x + 0.018) dx = 3.6 + 0.6 + 0.18 = 4.38 (in m · km²). Step 3, multiply by 10⁶: about 4.38 million cubic metres of water. Step 4, hydrologists compare such totals with river capacity for flood warnings. Real models are built from many gauge readings and numerical integration, but the idea is the same.

Real life example 2, blurring a photo: When a photo app applies a Gaussian blur, each new pixel becomes a weighted average of the nearby old pixels, with weights given by a 2D bell curve e^(-(x² + y²)/(2σ²)). In continuous form, the blurred image is a double integral of the original image times this weight, called a convolution. Computers approximate it by sums over pixels. The weights must add up to 1 so the picture does not get brighter or darker, and that normalising constant comes from the polar-coordinate Gaussian integral you just saw. Similar double and triple integrals appear in 3D rendering, where software integrates incoming light over directions to colour each pixel.

Common mistakes: Putting variables in the outer limits. Forgetting the extra r in polar coordinates or ρ² sin φ in spherical ones. Changing the order of integration without redrawing the region, which usually gives wrong limits. Integrating with respect to the wrong variable first, given the order of dx and dy. Using a type I description for a region that needs to be split into two parts. Forgetting the absolute value of the Jacobian.

What exams ask: Evaluate iterated integrals; sketch the region and change the order of integration; evaluate double integrals in polar coordinates; find areas and volumes with double integrals, such as the volume of a sphere, a cone or the region under a paraboloid; evaluate triple integrals over boxes, tetrahedra and cylinders; use the Jacobian for a change of variables; and prove ∫ e^(-x²) dx = √π using polar coordinates.

Recap: A double integral adds f over a region, giving volume under a surface when f ≥ 0. Compute it as an iterated integral, in either order for nice functions (Fubini), with the inner limits allowed to depend on the outer variable. Change the order by redrawing the region. Polar coordinates use dA = r dr dθ, and general substitutions use |J| du dv. Triple integrals measure volume and mass, with cylindrical and spherical coordinates for round solids. Next we finally turn to the equations that describe change itself: differential equations.
key_points: A double integral ∬_R f dA adds f over a region; for f ≥ 0 it is the volume under the surface.
Fubini: compute as iterated integrals in either order for continuous f; outer limits must be constants.
Type I regions: y between g₁(x) and g₂(x); type II: x between h₁(y) and h₂(y).
Change the order by redrawing the region, e.g. ∫₀¹∫ₓ¹ e^(y²) dy dx = (e - 1)/2.
Polar: dA = r dr dθ; the Gaussian integral ∫ e^(-x²) dx = √π comes from squaring and using polar coordinates.
General substitution: dA = |∂(x, y)/∂(u, v)| du dv.
Triple integrals: dV = dx dy dz; cylindrical dV = r dr dθ dz; spherical dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ.
Applications: area (f = 1), volume, mass, centre of mass, averages and probabilities.
lessons.tip: Never set limits for a multiple integral without a sketch. Draw the region, draw one strip in the direction of the inner integral, and read the limits off the ends of that strip.
lessons.task: Evaluate ∬ over the unit disk of (x² + y²) dA twice: once in Cartesian coordinates (try to set it up, notice the square roots) and once in polar coordinates. Compare how long each takes; the answer is π/2.
